LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): Mr. Speaker, may I inform this hon: house that a detachment made up of volunteers from the corps of Canadian fire fighters now in the British isles has been organized for service on the continent of Europe in support of our invading armies. speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Perhaps this is the proper place for me to make a correction in the statement which I made in answer to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Graydon) on July 10 with respect to disturbances at Petawawa. At the time I answered my hon. friend I found his question on my desk when I came into my office, and I went immediately to the telephone and got the information from the officers at headquarters. They gave me the information which I immediately gave the house in answer to the question. I now have the proceedings of the court of inquiry and the report of an investigation conducted by the officers of the department whom I directed to be sent to Petawawa, and I very much regret to find that the information I gave the house was not accurate.
I said that at the training centre commanded by Colonel Johnston the only disturbance in recent days had taken place about three weeks ago. I find, in fact, that there had been tw'o disturbances on successive nights; one on June 25 and the other on June 26. The incident on June 25 took place around nine o'clock that evening. A large group of approximately one hundred and fifty men had gathered close beside the canteen and there was some argument between some unidentified persons. I mention that particularly because I stated to my hon. friend that there were only two men involved in each case. The officer tells me that there were only two men involved in the fight, but at the same time I did not have the information that there was a crowd in addition to that. Hebert, a witness, states that he saw a scuffle and noticed a sergeant and a couple of other ranks lying on the ground. None of these has been identified. Another witness, Peters, a coloured man and a boxer, says he saw a few men "pick on" the sergeant. This latter witness did not know what the argument was about but he decided to participate in the scufile in order to help the sergeant, and he got into the fight and says that the crowd was arguing whether he was fighting for the general service or the N.R.M.A., and that he said he was not on 100-321
either side-all he wanted was fair play. Hebert, who had been acting as a regimental policeman, called the provost who intervened. The scuffle stopped almost immediately and the crowd moved off.
About twenty minutes later it appeared that a man named1 Dussault insulted! Hebert, the acting regimental policeman. There had been bad blood between them in the past arising from personal differences. No fight ensued, as friends on both sides stopped them. However, tempers had risen and Dussault incited the soldiers who were still there to get after Hebert; the latter and; two of his friends ran for safety in an office nearby. Most of the crowd followed and the office door was forced open and the upper panel broken. Hebert and his friends escaped by the window. At this time the crowd had increased and there were approximately two hundred men milling around. The regimental sergeant major and some senior non-commissioned officers arrived, ordered the men to proceed to their huts, which they did, and when the orderly officer arrived immediately afterward everything was under control. Hebert, one of the escaping men, reported to the medical inspection room with a lacerated nose. Dussault was the. only man identified in the group which forced the door, and he was disciplined. I may say as a matter of fact that Dussault was just back from embarkation leave. I think he is now overseas. Both Hebert and Dussault were general service men.
The second incident was about nine-thirty the next night. It is substantially as I stated last week. Two men, both general service soldiers, had been doing some drinking and got into an altercation but did not come to blows. A group of about fifteen soldiers got around them, and when the orderly officer ordered .them to break up they did so immediately. A little later a crowd of about fifty had gathered, apparently waiting for something to happen. There was some argument going on but no fight. After the canteen closed there would be probably two hundred' men around. The orderly officer was in the vicinity from nine-thirty onwards. He saw the men in their huts and the lights out. He stayed around until about eleven o'clock and when he left everything was quiet.
These are the incidents at training centre A-l commanded by Colonel Johnston. I had said there was only one disturbance, but as I have just indicated, there were disturbances on two different days. As I mentioned to the house, there had been an incident some time ago at training centre A-2. I said it was

Disturbances at Petawawa Camp

about two mouths ago. As a matter of fact it was on April 9, over three months ago. I said on the tenth that the rumour was that there was a fight between a general service and N.R. M.A. soldier. I find now that what happened was that a general service soldier got into a dispute with another general service soldier as a result of some objection he made to singing in French. He was ejected from the wet canteen by regimental police. It was just closing time, and after the crowdl had left the canteen they gathered outside. There was some shouting and noise which attracted men from the neighbouring huts. A crowd gathered, estimated at about a hundred and fifty men. The regimental sergeant major came on the scene and ordered the men to disperse, which they did. No one was injured, there was no fighting and no property damage.
It should be noted by the house that a crowd of two or three hundred men would not be at all unusual at canteen closing time in a large camp like Petawawa, where there are between nine thousand and ten thousand men.
The officer af Camp Petawawa who gave the information which I gave to the house explains the incompleteness of the telephone information on the ground that he had not then seen the proceedings of the inquiry. I would like to repeat that I received the question of the leader of the opposition only a few minutes before the opening of the house, and in my desire to answer promptly I immediately telephoned my officers here who gave me the information which I forthwith gave the house. This information had been forwarded to headquarters by telephone from Petawawa, and contained nothing showing that any crowd had been involved in the incidents referred to.
I should like to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that general service and N.R.M.A. personnel have been training together in probably seventy-five camps and schools all across Canada for over three years. There has been remarkably little in the way of friction. I think both the officers and the men are entitled to great credit for the way they have carried on.
In Petawawa, which is our second largest camp in Canada, there are more differences to be taken account of than in any other camp in the dominion. We can hardly expect that there would not be strained relations at times between N.R M.A. and general service personnel, but that is not by any means the only possible cause for quarrels, especially in camps of that size and where so many differences of various kinds exist. I am not going to minimize these episodes, but on the other

hand I do not think that we should add to the difficulties of loyal and faithful officers and staff who have to deal with men of all sorts and make them soldiers by undue emphasis on incidents like these, which might occur in any camp, especially around canteen closing time. I think the Petawawa camp has made on the whole an excellent reputation for order and for good work, and I am sure that both officers and other ranks want to help to keep it that way. I would ask the house and the country that we try to leave them to do it.

Will the coloured
soldier get a medal?

He may get the golden
gloves.

He went to the rescue
of the sergeant, did he not?

maintopic: ACCIDENT AT MOUNT BRUNO RANGES ON JULY 6

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: ACCIDENT AT MOUNT BRUNO RANGES ON JULY 6
speechtext:
May I refer to another question which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked me on July 10 with regard to the tragic accident at Mount Bruno. Immediately the accident occurred two things were done. The attorney general of the prov-

Disturbances at Calgary
ince of Quebec was notified; it was indicated to him that a court of inquiry would be held, and he was given the opportunity to have a representative at the court of inquiry. At the same time the coroner was notified. As a matter of fact the coroner did hold a coroner's inquest in respect of the twelve cases in which,, most regrettably, fatalities occurred.
The finding of the coroner's inquest in all twelve cases was as follows:
Concerning the death of 

 age - years,
domiciled at

; which death happened on the

 day of the month of

nineteen hundred
and forty-four at Montreal, a report haying been made to this court, an inquest was held by me on the 8th of July of the said year, and after having heard the relatives of -the deceased,
*the witnesses, and Doctor 

 who declared as
cause of the death 

And then comes the actual injury suffered by the deceased whose name is mentioned in the finding-
I came to the conclusion that the said 

died of a violent death; that this death was not imputable to the crime of whomsoever, neither to the negligence of anybody; that no crime accompanied or preceded this death, and there was no necessity to hold an inquest before a jury. In consequence, a verdict of an accidental death was rendered.	[DOT]
Pierre Hebert,
Joint Coroner of the District of Montreal.
This is simply the finding of the joint coroner of the district of Montreal.
A full opportunity was given the civil authorities to investigate the matter, and that finding was rendered in all twelve cases. As a matter of fact the findings in four of the cases were forwarded here a few days ago, and I think the remaining eight were received here yesterday.
May I now proceed to the matter of the court of inquiry itself. The attorney general replied on July 7 to the notice we gave him. The reply is as follows:
Your message received re inquiry on death of soldiers accidentally killed at Mount Bruno. Coroner having made an investigation not felt necessary to send representative to attend military court of inquiry.
This is signed by Mr. Cantin, K.C.
The qualifications of the members of the court were these: Major A. T. Stikeman belongs to A.48 basic training centre, artillery, stationed at St. Johns, Quebec. He has had much experience in courts of inquiry during the past two years, and has been eighteen years in commissioned service. Major J. H. Rankin is a permanent force soldier who enlisted in the R.C.O.C. in 1936 and qualified as an ammunition examiner in 1938. He was recommended by the officer commanding
Longue Pointe ordnance depot as being an expert ammunition man, the best available. Captain B. W. A. Allison is attached to A.12 infantry training centre. This officer belongs to the unit concerned. He has had four years' service in the present war and is a graduate in arts of the university of Edinburgh. In civil life he was assistant branch manager of a textile firm. He has had previous experience on courts of inquiry, and is well spoken of.
The court held a number of sittings-I do not know the number of witnesses, but it was a very large number.
I am now in a position to tell the house of the circumstances surrounding this unfortunate accident which took place at Mount Bruno Rifle Ranges, Mount Bruno, Quebec, on July 6, 1944.
The proceedings of the court of inquiry have been received and perused. The information disclosed is substantially as follows:
On July 6, 1944, a detachment of the specialist company, Canadian infantry training centre at Farnham, province of Quebec, went from Farnham to Mount Bruno ranges ta give a demonstration of mortar firing to personnel of Farnham at that time at the battLa drill camp at Mount Bruno.
The demonstration was supervised by an experienced mortar officer and a staff sergeant who had had long experience in firing 3-inch mortar.
The crew were picked men from a group of twenty-seven who had recently completed a qualifying course.
The 3-inch mortar used for the demonstration had been inspected by technical personnel of the army on the evening of the previous day and found in a clean and serviceable condition. The evidence does not indicate any use of the mortar between the time of the inspection and the demonstration.
The ammunition (mortar bombs) had been drawn that morning from the stores of the training centre at Farnham and had been obtained previously through ordnance at Montreal. This ammunition had been inspected in May, 1944, and found serviceable.
At 1120 a.m., a couple of hours before the actual demonstration, which took place at
1.45 p.m., a further check was made of the weapon and ammunition by the detachment commander of the gun crew and the members of the crew.
At the time set for the demonstration personnel under training at the battle drill camp,, consisting of 105 all ranks, were paraded to the site of the 3-inch mortar and took up positions from twenty-five to thirty feet from the mortar. They were placed as a company, in
Disturbances at Calgary

threes, in a semi-circle to allow every man to see what was going on. Four bombs were fired successfully; No. 2 of the gun crew was then seen placing the fifth bomb in the barrel of the mortar, whereupon a terrific explosion was heard and a large red flash was seen as well as black smoke at the site of the gun position. The gun crew were killed outright and a number of those watching the demonstration were wounded.
_ Medical assistance, both military and civilian, was immediately requested by telephone, and a Roman Catholic chaplain from the St. Hubert airport was called. There was a qualified medical orderly with a first aid kit on duty with the troops. Unfortunately he was one of those injured.
In the meantime all able personnel of all ranks administered first aid to the injured and field and shell dressings carried by all of the men as a part of their personal equipment were iused in addition to medical supplies furnished by the range caretaker. The court in its finding commended all ranks for their cool-headedness and intelligent care of the wounded.
Two civilian doctors were on the scene of the accident within twenty minutes after - the explosion but because of the adequate first aid already given found that only the administering of sedatives was required1.
I think I saw at one place where they had readjusted some temporary bandages as well. I do not wish to be tied down to that, but I believe I did see that-that they had rearranged the bandages. Ten minutes later the parish priest of Mount Bruno arrived with a Cistercian Father and administered religious rites to the dying. Ambulances and army medical personnel arrived about forty-five minutes after the blast, and the wounded were driven to various hospitals in Montreal immediately thereafter.
I very much regret to report that the casualty list at present is: 7 killed; 5 died of wounds; one critically injured; 16 severely injured, and 16 injured. One civilian, the caretaker, was injured.
The evidence establishes that the explosion took place in the base of the mortar, and the court so found.
It was impossible to establish conclusively from the few fragments of the bomb which were found that the bomb which exploded was defective. However the evidence indicates that the explosion was not due to any defect in the mortar itself or to improper technique on the part of the crew in loading the mortar. The elimination of these two possible causes of the explosion supports the explanation that
{Mr, Ralston.]
the cause was a defective bomb and the court so found.
All ammunition of this batch is impounded and will be returned for examination by X-ray.
That is the very terse report on the situation. It is all I am able to report at this time, with this addition, that I do wish to express my most profound regrets for the accident, and my deep sympathy to the bereaved families of the victims of this most unfortunate episode.
I can say to the house that as soon as this ammunition is X-rayed, if we find there is anything wrong with it I shall make a further report. As I understand it, this is ammunition of a certain fuse series, and that is all being taken and being retested.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA COAL MINING INDUSTRY-JOINT PRODUCTION COMMITTEE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA COAL MINING INDUSTRY-JOINT PRODUCTION COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour. Recently two members of the industrial cooperation board, Messrs Carl Goldenberg and M. M. Maclean, visited Nova Scotia to obtain first-hand information of the disabilities affecting the mining industry, and also for the purpose of setting up industrial production committees. Is the parliamentary assistant in position to report to the house as to the success or otherwise of that visit?

speakeroldname: Mr. PAUL MARTIN (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA COAL MINING INDUSTRY-JOINT PRODUCTION COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman gave me notice yesterday of his question, and in reply I wish to pay that in May and June, 1944, the industrial production cooperation board concluded agreements between the coal operators of Nova Scotia and district number 26 of the united mine workers of America for the formation of joint labour-management production committees in each mine and 'for the purpose of discussing all possibilities of improving and increasing coal production.
Following these agreements, Mr. H. Carl Goldenberg, chairman of the board, summoned a conference of the coal operators and of the miners to be held in Sydney, Nova Scotia, on July 12 and 13, with a view to inaugurating the joint production committee and to discuss
all aspects of the problems responsible for the decline in coal output, as well as possible means of increasing output.
Mr. Goldenberg and Mr. M. M. Maclean, a member of the board, proceeded to Sydney for these conferences. The conferences were attended by a large representation of both operators and miners. The conferences were marked by a full and frank discussion of the problems facing both operators and miners in the Nova Scotia coal mining industry. The discussions led to a clarification of a number of issues, and to a better understanding of mutual grievances.
The principal agreement reached at the conference was that both operators and miners undertook immediately to consider all causes, such as absenteeism, presently interfering with maximum coal production, at meetings of the joint production committees, the first of the series being held on Monday of this week, July 17. It was further agreed that meetings of these committees are to be held twice every month at each mine, and that the operators and the miners would submit for consideration to each meeting problems affecting coal production as each side sees them, together with recommendations for solutions or improvements. Each side also undertook to give immediate consideration to all recommendations, the operators to put such recommendations as are acceptable and feasible into effect as soon as possible, and the union to urge its members to act accordingly. Reports of these meetings and of the progress made are to be submitted regularly to the industrial production cooperation board, which will continue to assist in the operations of the committee in so far as is necessary.
The conference also discussed the recent closing down on Saturday morning of the two mines, number 4 and 11. The company advised that it was considering reopening these mines on Saturdays if the rate of absenteeism was reduced. Before the termination of the meetings the miners were advised by the Dominion Coal company that these two mines would be open on Saturday, July 15, and on that day they were open for work.
It is anticipated as a result of these conferences, and more particularly of the functioning of the joint production committee, that coal production problems will receive more immediate, more careful and more serious consideration. They will be considered both at the level of the mine production committee and of the district production committee, the latter covering a number of mines. H both parties show the good will and cooperation which they showed at the conferences attended



Labour Conditions
by Messrs. Goldenberg and MacLean, there should be an improvement in the coal situation,. The industrial production cooperation board now has this matter in hand, and will follow up on the conferences as the situation requires it.
I may say the conferences in. Nova Scotia are in accordance with the policy laid down by the government sponsoring the formation of labour-management production committees in industry. A large number of these committees are now functioning across Canada, and the staff of the industrial production cooperation board is constantly engaged in setting up more of these committees. Not only in the coal mines, but in all industry, joint production committees should constitute effective machinery for the discussion and solution of production problems by labour and management on a democratic basis.

subtopic: NOVA SCOTIA COAL MINING INDUSTRY-JOINT PRODUCTION COMMITTEE
speechtext: I want to thank the parliamentary assistant for the very comprehensive reply he has given, and I also want to compliment the department for the realistic action they are taking at the present time in connection with this matter.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour. speakeroldname: Mr. PAUL MARTIN (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: NATIONAL WAR LABOUR BOARD-APPLICATION OP STANDARD RAILWAY LABOUR ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman gave me notice of his question. While it is not possible to give the hon. member any specific date on which the decision of the national war labour board on this case will be made known, I can assure the hon. member that the national war labour board has this matter under active consideration. I should like to say further that this is a complex case involving detailed and careful analyses of wage rates and related matters. I should like to point out that the delay which is apparent in the date cited by the hon. member in his question has arisen from two factors. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee is on resolution 2 of the succession duty act.
2.	That when a person is given a general power of appointment or disposal over property, such property be subject to duty as if it were given directly to him, and, upon his death, the person then benefiting be regarded as his successor for purposes of taxation.
[Mr. Ilsley.l

Mr. Chairman, I desire to go to the banking committee very shortly and I should like to make one or two inquiries now with respect to this resolution.
Last night brief consideration was given to this resolution and a case was cited by the hon. member for York West of what amounted' to confiscation by the action of the succession duty acts in the various provinces. In reply to a question by the hon. member for Saskatoon City the parliamentary assistant stated yesterday that the present resolution was to cover a technical omission from the act; that it was to take care of the case where a general power of appointment is given and the man does nothing about it. That of course is not quite apparent from the terms of the resolution itself, and I was fearful that the result of the change would be two taxes on the same set of funds. I think the resolution is open to that interpretation. Those of us who are lawyers and accustomed to draft wills know that it is a common thing for a testator to give to a person a general power of appointment or disposal over property, whether that person takes anything out of the fund or not. Frequently the person to whom the power is given is. also the recipient in his lifetime of income under the fund, and in such cases, I assume, his interest in the fund is taxable, having regard to the expectation of his life, and so on. A general power of appointment is given. But I have never seen a case where, in a testamentary disposition, the testator failed to give an alternative if the person in whom the power of appointment is vested fails to act. Usually there is an alternative. In my own practice I have invariably made it a rule to advise my clients that when the power of appointment is given to a particular person to dispose of a fund, on his death or at any intervening period, if he fails to act, the testator himself or herself in the will should proceed to make the disposition.
If I understand correctly the object of this resolution it is that if a person is given a general power of appointment or disposal, such property shall be subject to duty as if given directly to him; then upon his death, "the person then benefiting" will "be regarded as his successor for purposes of taxation." If that means anything it means two taxes on the same fund. There can be no question about it. I think that is wrong and unjust and should not become effective. I see the commissioner shaking his head, but I entirely disagree with that form of denial. That is what this means. It may be that that is not the intention, but it ought to be made absolutely clear either that it is or is not the intention of

Succession Duty
this resolution, so that the public will know just where it stands. To-day such a fund is in effect liable only to one tax. That tax may be divisible, if I may use that term. If. the person to whom a power of appointment is given takes any interest out of the fund, his interest in the fund is taxed, if I apprehend the law correctly, and the balance is taxable in the hands of the party to whom it is disposed. Now, what is the position and what is the intention under this act?-because as it stands to-day this fund is going to be taxed twice. Parliament ought to understand what the intention is, and so far as I am concerned I would oppose it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I speak on this with some
diffidence because I do not .practise law in a common-law .province and I am not so familiar with this general power of appointment, although we have a similar provision in Quebec. I am advised it is not the intention of this section that there should be a double tax imposed. If property is conveyed under a general power of appointment with power to the person to whom it is conveyed to appoint himself, then there is a tax. Of course if he appoints himself and if the .property is still in existence at the time of his death it would vest in his heirs and be subject to tax.
Of course that is a very unusual case.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is a very unusual case,
but this is intended to prevent that. The form of the act,.as my hon. friend knows, defines under section 3 what is a succession; and in the dominion act we have rather followed the practice in the various provinces of an elaborate definition, if you will, of what is included in a succession.

On the
theory that you do not want to leave anything out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Quite so, and also partly
because of certain decisions of the privy council with respect to the constitutional powers of the provinces to. tax. Section 3, subsection 1, sets out what a succession shall be deemed to include, and it includes a long list of various things,-property taken as a donatio mortis causa, and so on. Coming to paragraph (i) of subsection 1 of section 3 there is included in the definition or description of a succession-
-property of which the person dying was at the time of his death competent to dispose.
That is a common provision.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If property is left to one
person with power of appointment and if it is not exercised, then on his death, to a designated person: I think that is a common type of power of appointment. But if the power to appoint were general without a designated person to take the property, in the event of failure to exercise such power, and the power was not exercised, I am advised that as the section now stands the property may pass on the death and not be subject to tax.

That is
on the death of the testator?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Correct-on the death of
the first testator.
Ultimately it must pass to somebody.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
And the amendment is to
make certain that the .property passing on death even in the circumstances outlined would be taxable. It is pretty technical to me.

Let us understand this, because it is perpetuating what they have in New Brunswick-or so I am informed; I have not the statute before me-and it is something I have never ceased! to protest against. There is a double tax down there under these conditions; at least my colleague the hon. member for St. John-Albert tells me that is so and I take his word for it. That just means this, that on the death of the testator the whole fund pays the tax, under the present proposal, irrespective of to whom it may pass. It is a particular kind of fund which is not disposed of by the testator except in certain contingencies. Then, if the person to whom the power of appointment is given-if I understand the position correctly; I am rather feeling my way along-fails to make operative the power which is vested in. him by the testamentary instrument, and no alternative has been provided in the testamentary instrument, another tax is imposed* Is that the position?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.
When it vests in a third person. That is the position.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There would really be another transmission under these circumstances which would not have flowed from the direction of the original testator.

That, I think, clarifies what is intended, although it is somewhat involved. Now, if the testator has a fund over which he gives a power of appointment to, say, the husband-most frequently I think it happens in the case of
Succession Duty

a wife or a husband having a fund for the benefit of children, and they do not like to designate the w'hole of them, or they want to keep them on good behaviour-that has been my experience-it goes to the one most worthy and perhaps cuts out somebody who is unworthy, if the testator makes an alternative disposition; in the event of failure of the appointee then there is not a second tax.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct.
There is not a second tax. I hope I am right about that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am certain about it.
Then, of course, what people should do is to look at their wills. Now I understand the proposal. It is based on this theory that there are two successions; is that the idea?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct.
Based on the theory of two successions?

speechtext: I think this discussion has been useful. Perhaps the committee would defer further discussion until we have the bill before us and the exact text of the proposed amendment which will fit in with the section of the act which it is intended to amend. When the bill is in committee the succession dirty experts of the committee who are familiar with this branch of the law could carefully scrutinize it.
I agree with the parliamentary assistant that it would be very much better if we had the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It would be easier for us to discuss it.
I think I understand the principle.

If a man by his will leaves his property to his wife for life .with the power of appointment, and, failing to exercise that power, then to his children share and share alike, when the testator dies is there a tax imposed on his widow on the full value of his estate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext:
She pays on her life interest in the estate, and in Quebec-I do not know
(Mr. R. B. Hanson.]
about the dominion-it is based on her life expectancy. As to the subsequent transmission to the children, that, of course, was not in virtue of any general power of appointment given to the widow, but was provided for by the testator himself, and on her death this proposed amendment would have no relation to that situation whatsoever.
I do not know; there is a power of appointment there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: But not a general power of appointment. The power of appointment, as my hon. friend will see when the legislation is brought down, is power of appointment where an absolute discretion is given to the testator and no provision made as to whom the property should go in the event of his failing to exercise that power.

The resolution reads:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This resolution may not be very happily framed. I have tried to make clear that what he appears to fear is not the intention of the resolution. The bill will be drafted-drafting may be almost complete now-along those lines: I suggested a moment ago in the discussion with the hon. member for York-Sunbury that perhaps we could make the criticism a little more effective if we deferred it until we had reached the sections of the bill in committee. I do not want to force that view on. the committee, but I should prefer to discuss it with the section before me.
I quite agree with the parliamentary assistant, but I wish to make this point clear. Where the property is given with a general power of appointment, no restrictions-[DOT]

In the power of appointment he may express certain wishes in the will. And as 1 understand it from the way this is worded the estate is immediately taxed on the whole value.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Right.
If he exercises the general power of appointment then the whole estate is taxed again upon his death?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right.

I want to make that point clear. It would be a very foolish thing for a lawyer ever to draw a will along those lines.

29. Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and water storage, $2,000,000.

This item was quite fully discussed the other day, particularly with respect to larger schemes which might be carried out in western Canada under this act. We all agree that these larger schemes have their place, but I think the act was originally drafted for the purpose of taking care of the smaller schemes-dugouts, regrassing, the forming of community pastures and that type of work. As such it has performed a very useful service in western Canada, and has done a great deal of good. However I should like to see this scheme extended much further than it goes at the present time. It has been maintained to a great extent in what is known as the Palliser triangle in Saskatchewan. That
is, as a matter of fact, the old drought area. In northern Saskatchewan we have gone into stock raising on a large scale, and we have found that in many parts of that area, since the land has been cleared and the bush taken off, many of the streams which formerly ran through the whole of the season now run only during about two months in the early part of the season. The matter of obtaining a water supply in some of the northern areas not now included under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has become a serious problem. Many of the municipalities are now making application to come under the act. I suggest serious consideration should be given to those applications, and that perhaps they should be considered before some of the larger schemes are entered into. If many of these municipalities could obtain the proper machinery for the digging of these dugouts, I know they would be very glad to enter into some sort of agreement with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act administration to do this type of work in those municipalities in the northern part of the province.
I know the minister has received applications from that part of Saskatchewan, and that he has given sympathetic consideration to some of them. However, there are still many others anxious to come in under the act. I bring this to his attention, and ask again that serious consideration be given this matter.
The other matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention is one which was discussed by the hon. member for Acadia. I refer to the division of the water rights in the whole Saskatchewan river area. We in the northeast part of the province are possibly most interested in the power projects which might be developed from that river. If some of the larger schemes of irrigation are entered into in the western part of Saskatchewan and in Alberta they might seriously curtail the amount of water available for power purposes at points farther along the river. I would certainly suggest to the minister that at as early a date as possible an interprovincial conference should be held with respect to this matter, and that possibly a commission should be set up to come to some agreement in respect of the division of the water available. There is no doubt that by the establishment of reserves in the foothills a much more economical use could be made of the water than is being made at the present time. But before too much expense is involved in connection with the surveying and laying out of these larger schemes, it is my view that some agreement should 'be arrived at between the provinces. Otherwise it is just possible that some
Supply-Agriculture

of the survey expenses which may be incurred and other necessary work connected with these larger schemes, would be useless, if there is not enough water available.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
Before replying to the points raised by the hon. member I should like to emphasize a correction in a report which has gone out from the discussion which took place the other day. I notice that in some of the press I am credited with having advised the committee that farmers should hold back their cattle. I think hon. members who were in the committee will agree that no such suggestion was made in the discussions which took place the other day. I should like to emphasize the fact that we do not want cattle held back. On the contrary we want cattle marketed at this time-all cattle, in fact, that are ready to 'be marketed, in order to avoid bringing about a great glut on the market later on, in October. We feel that in October the rush of hogs will take up a considerable part of the capacity of the packing plants, and for that reason we would like cattle to be passed through in as large numbers as possible ' before that time. So that I wish just to emphasize the fact that I had no intention of even suggesting toi the committee or the country that the farmers should hold back their cattle.
On the question the hon. member for Mel-fort has now brought 'before the committee, may I say that in principle I agree with what he has said, namely, that we should emphasize small projects. I think it is generally agreed that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was brought into being to assist individual farmers as much as possible in areas where they were experiencing difficulty in getting water for live stock or water for small irrigation projects which might provide them with feed and fodder. That was the original intention of the act, and considerable emphasis should be placed upon that feature at all times. We did experience difficulty in getting the money spent on these small projects. The hon. member for Melfort will recall that that was the condition in the early stages of the development of this plan. The first act indicated that the farmer himself should dig the dugout. He was told under the terms of the act and the regulations that if he did so about half the cost-in the first place it was a third, and later it was raised to a half, then later to two-thirds, and then at last reduced to a half again-would be borne by the government. He was told that if he would put

up approximately half the cost, the government would pay the other half. That was the way we started.
In the first year it was found that there were very few farmers who dug the dugouts, the chief reason being that they did not have the equipment. It will be recalled that at that time we had drought and poor crops, with resulting poor feed supplies. Even those farmers who could secure equipment from the municipalities did not have horses fed to the condition where they could be utilized for that kind of heavy work. And so the farmers just said, "We are not able to do it."
Then we devised a plan of encouraging municipalities to obtain equipment, either by hiring contractors or by buying equipment themselves and taking out the bottom six or seven feet. They said, "If the farmer takes off the first five feet they would send draglines in to take out the other six or seven feet." The money which would otherwise have gone to the farmers was paid to the municipality or to the contractor.
It will be recalled that in 1939 we had an unfortunate experience with that. We had authorized the digging of dugouts by the thousands. The farmer was authorized to go ahead and dig any time he wished to do so. In the early stages there were very few dug, and the result was that we did not get into financial difficulties. But in 1939 when there was a shortage of work for drag-lines and construction equipment, practically every contractor in the country entered into the digging of dugouts. It will be recalled that it took us two years to pay for the dugouts dug in 1939. As a matter of fact, a great many of our opponents said, unkindly, that we did it because there was an election coming on. Of course no one knew in 1939 that there was going to be an election in the winter of 1940. We did not even know it ourselves. Even in this house we did not know it until one day in January. Nevertheless, those who like to produce political arguments said that we simply went out and dug all these dugouts- twice as many as we could pay for-in that year, because there was an election coming on in the winter of 1940. We were not able to dig any dugouts in the summer of 1940 because we had no money with which to dig them. We had to pay for those already dug.
We are coming back into a similar period. For the last three or four years every contractor has been busy working on airfields and other work of that kind and was not able to dig any dugouts. In the meantime the municipalities have been buying equipment or have been getting permits to buy equipment in

Supply-Agriculture
order to do this work. Some contractors have equipment not now working on new work. The result is that this year there are many people who want to dig dugouts. The municipalities have equipment and the contractors are coming back and are trying to get work digging dugouts. The money was expended by the middle of July this year.
There was just as much money for dugouts as there has been in other years. Under ordinary circumstances we would not have been able to spend any more money than we spent last year or the year before, but my information is that this year the money ceased to exist about the middle of July. I think another $30,000 was provided in order to make it possible to go on until about harvest time. It is not entirely a question of how much money was available. We tried to divide the money up in such a manner as to get it all spent on useful undertakings, but it requires a lot of cooperation and sometimes a lot of advance knowledge as to what equipment is going to be available and so on. This year we could probably have used more money on dugouts than we have if we had known in advance that there was going to be equipment available.

Are the contractors who
formerly did this work going to continue to do it this year? What price per yard is being paid and is it the same as it always was?
It was estimated that it took about nine cents per yard to move the earth, and we are paying four and a half cents per yard.
At the present time?

Yes, and we have been for three years. For a time we did pay up to six cents but we reduced it because we found that certain of these people who had purchased equipment could dig dugouts for six cents per yard, and in certain cases municipalities which had purchased equipment could dig them for that price. We were a little suspicious that in some cases they were making money digging them, and we put it back to four and a half cents, which has been the price for three years.

I believe considerable survey work has been done in the Qu'Appelle valley and the tributaries of the Qu'Appelle. The minister will know what I mean by " tributaries." Some stock watering dams were built. Is there anything likely to be carried on following the results of those surveys? Could the minister give us a little information with respect to the surveys and the reports he got?

The general plan in connection with any of these streams in the west is that we put in engineering parties to make surveys. We have done considerable work on the Frenchman1 river and in the southeastern part of the province where we are carrying on similar projects. Some of these surveys were originally carried on by the provincial government when irrigation was entirely under the provincial government, and we continued the survey work. Surveys were carried on on the South Saskatchewan river for the purpose of locating projects similar to the one which had been developed at Medicine Hat. There is a privately operated irrigation project just outside of Medicine Hat where the water is pumped up about sixty feet to a plateau which can be irrigated. Corn and alfalfa and other crops are grown there in abundance. With that experience and with the experience gained from other projects we conceived the idea of trying to locate as many as possible of these along the South Saskatchewan river between Medicine Hat and Saskatoon. Survey parties have been out working on this. From these, information can be supplied to farmers along the way as to what can be done.
Such projects can be developed only if power is available. We have all the figures of the cost of operating the project at Medicine Hat. Power is supplied there and there has been a discussion of the possibility of the company that develops power on the Bow river up at Calgary extending its line right on through to Saskatoon. They have asked for the privilege of doing this on a number of occasions. This kind of project is involved in the kind of thing that as now being discussed in Saskatchewan. It is suggested that all power development in Saskatchewan shall be under government control. About fifty per cent of it is now under government control. That would make it necessary for the government rather than the company to continue on through to Saskatoon. The Saskatoon plant is operated by the government. There would have to be power lines before these developments could be carried on along this particular stream.
Similar investigations are being made along the Qu'Appelle. I think survey parties have been out continuously for the last five years and as a result recommendations have been made in connection with the controlling of the waters in the lakes in the Qu'Appelle valley. Dams have been constructed at Buffalo Pound lake and at Long lake as well as at Qu'Appelle lake near the town of Fort Qu'Appelle. These dams control the waters in the Qu'Appelle valley. As is known by all who are familiar with that valley, Buffalo Pound lake is the
Supply-Agriculture

first of a series in the valley. At times when there is a rush of water the level of this lake is at a certain level. As the season advances and evaporation occurs the water level will drop from three to six feet below the level of the outlet. The water then became just standing water with no stream flowing out of the lake. A dam has been built across the end of the lake which prevents the water from rushing out in the spring. This dam is opened during the summer months to permit a continuous stream of water down the river. That is the object of having the dam there.
A little further along the valley is Long lake. This was probably not a part of the Qu'Appelle river but in a tributary basin. If one flies over the country he will see that at one time there must have been a connection between Long lake and Quill lake. There are alkali flats between those two lakes which indicate that they may have been lakes which have filled in at some time. The water flows into Long lake out of the Qu'Appelle valley in the early spring, and later sometimes flows out by the same runway as it flowed in. During a drought period Long lake may be six feet below the level at which water flows out. No water flowed out for a number of years recently because the level of the lake surface was too low. We have controls now at the end of that lake which we hope will result in our being able to control the level of the water to better advantage when the water in the lake returns to the level at which it once was.
Below that are the Qu'Appelle lakes. At the town of Qu'Appelle, where the old grade ran across the river and where the original bridge was, there is a dam put in. The grade was already there. When the dam was put in, the waters in that lake were kept up from one and a half to two feet, at any rate to a higher level than they were before. It is impossible to keep the waters any higher than the dam provides for because all along that lake we have summer resorts and people with cottages and if the water were higher certain points being utilized as summer resorts would be washed away.
The parties working along these lakes were providing information upon which decisions could be reached as to the levels at which the water should be controlled.
The next lake below Qu'Appelle is Katpewe lake. There has been a dam at the end of that lake for many years and the water is still kept at the same level at which it was prior to this programme being undertaken. But it is suggested by the engineers that the level should be raised. We have doubts about that because of the experience we have had. 
When I was minister of highways in Saskatchewan we put another foot on top of the dam and then had to take it off because the water was beginning to wash away the lands where the church and cemetery and Indian school buildings are located at Lebret. So that we had to let more of the water out of the lake. We are getting expert information from the engineers which will enable us to avoid difficulties such as we have got into in the past when trying to control the waters of that lake.
At Round lake and at Crooked lake it is much the same thing. There has been a dam constructed there for that purpose.
So far as the other surveys are concerned, they are made on streams running into the Qu'Appelle valley from both sides. Those streams have flowing water in them, under natural conditions, only in the spring of the year. The grade on which the stream flows is steep and the waters have a rapid descent. What the engineers are doing is trying to find all the locations where one could put in a dam and hold the water sufficiently far back to make it useful for different purposes, one of them being stock watering, as has been suggested. A number of small stock watering dams have been put in on different streams. What the engineers are really searching for is locations where one could put a dam across what may be a flat that runs out from one of these streams, and back the water into it in very much the same way as the water backs into Long lake.
In other words, make reservoirs.

Yes, instead of having the water come down in the spring months, in a rush that will be over in from two to six week's time, we are attempting to hold the water back and let it down the streams gradually, keeping the water in the lakes at the bottom of the valley up to the proper level and keeping the stream flowing during: the summer months instead of its being converted into stagnant pools.
The idea would be to have more than one dam on each stream.

Our big difficulty is not as to the number, but finding the proper locations. Because of the rapid descent of the streams, one could put a dam in it anywhere and hold back the water for two or three hundred feet, but we are trying to find a location where we can hold the water back for half a mile or a mile. If that can be-done on the stream itself, so much the better. Where we can find locations to put in a dam,.

Supply-Agriculture
say ten feet high, which would put six feet of water in a reservoir along the ravines, we would do that.
'Mr. MacNICOL: They are working on that now?

Yes. These survey parties which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is asking about have been working continuously on that and we have some reports on locations where that can be done. The streams come in from both the north and the south of the river.

'If I may interrupt the minister, three or four years ago there was the idea of using this water for irrigation purposes and encouraging the farmers to produce sugar beets in the valley. Has the minister any information on that?

That is a possibility, but if you are going to do that it will be necessary to have all your data on how much water you could store back and let down. One of the difficulties in that valley is that many flats that might be useful have been created through the disappearance of the water. There may have been a lake there but the silt nas come down and gradually filled up the lake until it is slightly above the high water mark of the stream, and the water disappears from the flat. There is some difficulty about irrigating a flat of that kind unless you can control water higher up the stream. You could not take sufficient water out of some of these lakes at present levels to irrigate any considerable acreage unless you had a further supply of water which you could let down after you had taken off your first supply of water. All that is being studied before any considerable scheme of irrigation can be entered upon. At present our information is that there is about 30,000 acres of land in that valley which could be irrigated if we were assured of a water supply and storage at the proper places.
In addition to irrigation down in the valley, there are many farmers along the tributaries who have possible projects very similar to those I spoke of on the Saskatchewan river, where a man by putting in a pumping outfit could pump water out on to a flat so that he would be assured of a garden, or it might irrigate a hay meadow without pumping. That is possible at places along these streams.

Does the minister recall that at Round lake and at Crooked lake a dam was put in raising the level of the water between four and five feet? That resulted in the flooding of the flats on the Indian reserve and destroying their hay meadows. They used to get about 500 or 600 tons of hay off that land
just west of the lake, but for the last two or three years they have not been able to get any hay from that land, and that has been a terrible blow to the Indians. I have taken that matter up with the Minister of Mines and Resources, and I have had two delegations from the reserve wait on me within the last six months urging me to continue my representations to the minister that the water be lowered, say three feet, draining certain areas, so that the Indians could produce the quantity of hay which they produced previously. But the Minister of 'Mines and Resources would not give these representations any consideration at all. I have been over the location and know exactly the situation. Will the Minister of Agriculture take it into consideration? It would not affect the water in the Qu'Appelle river because, as the minister knows, that is a flat country, and1 the water level in the other lakes would not be affected either. There would be no less water going from the Qu'Appelle lakes into the river. I wish the minister would give this matter his earnest consideration. As I said before, I cannot get any consideration from the other department; and as the minister's department is building the dams and controlling the water, I bring it to his attention now.

The Indian branch of the Department of Mines and Resources, of course, put in claims on account of that land, and we have paid them S3,330 in damages on account of these lands which were flooded by the putting in of the dam. I can understand that that does not get them the hay.

They protested against that, as the settlement which the department offered to make them was permanent and for all time. They said that would not reimburse their loss for any more than one or two years. Certainly they will lose the hay for all time, so to speak, and that is one of the reasons they protest against having been forced to accept that settlement. I asked the Minister of Mines and Resources if his department would reconsider it. No, they said, that offer had been made and the Indians had to accept it. It was forced on them, and they accepted it under protest.

What we actually do is buy the land. In all cases, whether it is individuals or the Department of Indian Affairs or any one else concerned, we set a price for the land and buy it; and of course the land is sometimes flooded and is under water for all time to come and no one can occupy it afterwards; it is occupied by a
Supply-Agriculture

lake. I am not just sure what the condition is at that point, whether the water is up over the land at all times.
It is now.
I presume we bought and paid for it, and it is now .part of the project.

I may say that the water is over it now, and the raising of the dam has forced a good many of the campers to move their cottages back. It is a great injustice to them; it has given them no additional service nor has it made the resort any more convenient or pleasurable.

Will the minister state how many municipalities have made applications to come under the P.F.R.A. which the government has been unable to accept, and what is the possibility of more of these municipalities being able to come under the scheme?

The present position is that we have taken in certain river basins which I think everyone will agree are more or less in the drought area. This legislation is based first upon the fact that there is a drought area, and in defining it we have kept as close as possible to what is known as the old Palliser triangle. When we started out to operate under the act first we were not able to define exactly the boundaries of the old Palliser triangle, and we adopted the idea of confining it to river basins. What we have taken is the Assiniboine river basin, the Qu'Appelle river basin, the Souris, the Frenchman, the South Saskatchewan, and the North Saskatchewan until it comes to the point where it joins the South and becomes the Saskatchewan river. We have taken the height of land east and north of these and have made that the boundary as far as Saskatchewan and Manitoba are concerned. On the Alberta side we have followed down between the streams from Lloydminster toward Calgary where we touch the foothills, and then followed the foothills down to the United States boundary. That, roughly speaking, is the boundary line around the area. It starts just north of Winnipeg, comes up west of lake Manitoba, then follows into Saskatchewan, and around the height of land dividing the Assiniboine river from the Saskatchewan river basin including the Crooked, which is a branch of the Saskatchewan, and following the height of land through to a point where a line drawn north joins the Saskatchewan river. We have gone around the northern side of the municipal boundaries wherever we can, rather than taking the south side. Where the height of land runs through the municipality we have invariably

taken the northern boundary. At the point where directly south of the junction of the two Saskatchewan rivers it becomes to Saskatchewan river, the boundary runs up to the junction of those rivers and then on the north side follows the height of land between the North Saskatchewan and the Churchill or other rivers north of the North Saskatchewan. That brings us out at the boundary line of Alberta at about where the North Saskatchewan river crosses the boundary line from Alberta into Saskatchewan. Municipalities all along that boundary line have suggested that they would like to be in, but our difficulty in connection with that is that a matter of policy is involved. The bill says, and all the discussions in this house have been related to the fact that, there is a drought area in the Palliser triangle and that because we induced settlers to go into it we ought to do something to assist in rehabilitating them; and that is the reason the act has the name it has.
A recommendation was made by a committee of this house last year that the principle should be applied to all lands and all provinces right across the country. The conflict is as between those two principles. If we are going to continue to apply this act to the Palliser triangle or-what is known as the drought area, then of course the problem of water conservation outside of it is the responsibility of the provinces. We at one time under the Saskatchewan government had a well-digging policy; and we also built dams all over Saskatchewan before this policy came in at all. The same thing was done in Alberta and Manitoba. You can find dams all over the drought area which were built by provincial governments before this plan was adopted. You can find wells on road allowances which were dug by the old territorial government before there was a province and that are still operating, and other wells which were dug, within the first years after the provinces were formed, by the provincial governments. In other words, the responsibility for that kind of thing has always been assumed to be a provincial responsibility, and the only place we have departed from that in this house is in connection with what we call the Palliser triangle, the drought area, and we only took that on during the recent drought period, on the assumption that the federal government had induced people to go there, knowing that it was a dry area.
I as minister, and many others in this house, would be in favour of having a policy which extended right across the country, provided we could adopt it without getting into great difficulties with the provinces. But for the time being, with this act as it is, and with the

Supply-Agriculture
discussions which have taken place in this house in carrying out these projects, we think it is impossible for us to go outside the Palliser triangle or the lands which are as nearly as possible related to the Palliser triangle.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

When the committee rose I was on the point of asking the minister a question with reference to what the prairie farm rehabilitation board is planning for that area west of the northern portion of the south branch of the Saskatchewan river west from Saskatoon. Last summer I met some engineers in the west who told me that the prairie farm rehabilitation board-to my mind quite rightly; I wish to support their plans in a general way-were planning to build a dam across the south branch of the Saskatchewan river at some point near Saskatchewan Landing. There is a natural depression north from that point, as the minister knows, which would seem to have been put there by Providence for some purpose. The depression is about forty miles long. A dam at Saskatchewan Landing, or perhaps near there, between 130 and 150 feet high, if the base of the river is of such material that a dam could be built that high, would result in that depression some forty miles long filling up with water. I believe that the general level would reach about 1,930 feet above sea level. If that could be done, the engineers really have something worth while. They could then run a canal north from a lake at the end of the depression, the name of which has slipped my mind at the moment; I think it is White Bear lake. The water level of that White Bear extension of the natural coulee would rise to about 1,930 feet above sea level. That would be providential, in my judgment. They propose to run a canal from the end of White Bear lake north for a few miles and then divide it into two main branches, one running northwest in the general direction of Tramping lake for perhaps fifty miles or more. Tramping lake is nothing more than a coulee at the moment. There is water in it at times and it is dry at times. Fortunately the general topography of the ground lends itself to these plans. In other, -words it slopes, I am told, from the high point of 1,930 feet down towards Tramping lake. If those plans are carried out it would mean that the water would flow by gravity as far as the Tramping lake depression. It would assist all of that area around Rose-town and the communities north. If my
memory serves me rightly the other branch of the canal runs off to the right in the general direction of Saskatoon and north of the general direction of Saskatoon towards a place called Kinley. Another branch is planned to turn southeast in the direction of Luck lake, west of Riverhurst. Riverhurst is on the opposite side of the south Saskatchewan river.
As it was explained to me, there were three areas that could be served for irrigation purposes with water from a reservoir built behind a dam in the vicinity of Saskatchewan Landing. The west area would be something over 200,000 acres. That great extent of land could be irrigated. The land that could be irrigated west of Saskatoon would consist of over 600,000 acres. The southeast area down in the direction of but west of Riverhurst would be something less than 100,000 acres. From the information I gathered from the engineers I judged that there would be at least a total of a million acres of land there that could be irrigated if a dam were erected at or near Saskatchewan Landing.
I wish to assure the minister as one hon. member of this house that if such a proposal to irrigate a million acres were put forward I would support it to the best of my ability. It would mean the opening up of many thousands of new farms. It would mean the irrigating of that area by gravity without pumping, as I understand it. I hope I am right in that. It would supply water to an area that richly deserves it. I believe if such a programme were carried out it would result in the doubling of the population of Saskatoon in twenty-five years. Instead of being a city of forty to fifty thousand people it could have ambitions of reaching a hundred thousand.
Other proposals, as the minister knows, have been made for bringing water four hundred miles from the north Saskatchewan river for irrigation purposes. I am opposed to that. I am opposed to any diversion from the north Saskatchewan river, and would do my best to organize opposition to it. But the scheme I have outlined seems to me to be one that Providence has provided for.
I ask the minister if any plans have been prepared to take care of providing water from a dam anywhere in the vicinity of Saskatchewan Landing for the irrigating of the million acres of the low moisture land west of the general line of Saskatoon and north of the general line from Saskatchewan Landing. If there are, they would have my sincere support. If the proposal to build the dam at Saskatchewan Landing-<a power dam as well as an irrigation dam, because the large coulee would store all the water that would be required to take care of the irrigation work,
Supply-Agriculture

and the dam itself would be of such a height that I believe some 75,000 horse-power could be produced there-is proceeded with it will have my support. However, I wish to warn the minister in one particular. As I see it, the primary consideration is the building of the other dam I proposed somewhere near River-hurst to take care of that area in the general [DOT]direction of Regina. I am not going to go into that, other than to say this. The engineers in charge of both those proposals should see to it that the dam at Saskatchewan Landing should not be so constructed that it would interfere with the backwater from' a dam that could be built near Riverhurst. By river water it would not be more than a hundred miles from Riverhurst to Saskatchewan Landing. I believe that the river level at Riverhurst is about 1,700 feet above sea level. I believe the river level at Saskatchewan Landing is about 1,811 feet above sea level. Therefore if the dam is raised to 1,930 feet the engineers would have to be careful that anything they do at Saskatchewan Landing would not interfere in any way with what must be done at Riverhurst. The first thing to be done is to build a dam somewhere near Riverhurst.
I wish to compliment the department on the grand plans that the P.F.R.A. people have apparently examined into. I can see plainly that if these plans were carried out, as they should be, with the cost divided in proportion, it would be a great thing for the central province of Saskatchewan.

The engineers of the P.F.R.A. branch are making surveys in the area just referred to by the hon. member for Davenport. The first investigations have to do with the possibility of building a dam somewhere near Saskatchewan Landing. Last year a certain amount of money was spent in [DOT]drilling test holes during the time the ice was on the river, in order to determine whether or not conditions were suitable for the construction of a dam. That is about as far as we have gone up to the present in the matter of investigations. There is no report from which I can quote as to what are the possibilities. The statement that has been made was a general statement of the situation as it now exists. This summer we hope to spend some money in making surveys from the air and further surveys on the ground in order to ascertain the possibilities of that plan, but at the moment I am not in a position to give any details of what will be accomplished by the plan or what are its possibilities for the future, because as yet we have not received a report from the engineers which would make such a statement possible. I

should add that the distance from the proposed site north of Moose Jaw to the site suggested here is something like sixty miles.
Am I right in my understanding that the general topography of the land slants to the north?
I would think so, though I have not an engineer's report upon which to base that statement. I believe water will have to be pumped in order to get it up to the point where it will flow.
Pumped out of the river?

Yes, I would think so.
I believe under the plan sufficient power will be developed from the dam itself to take care of the pumping, and the cost will not be prohibitive. I believe some pumping will have to be done, but I would not want to be too definite on that before we get the final report.

This vote is to support prairie farm rehabilitation, the need for which was recognized long years ago. Ten years ago the need became particularly acute, and this act was passed. That need is still great, particularly in the Palliser triangle, which so desperately requires something in the nature of a permanent policy. Year after year it has been demonstrated that there is not sufficient rainfall in that district to permit agriculture to be carried on, so that some permanent policy must be adopted in regard to irrigation. Streams flow eastward from the Rocky mountains and north from the Cypress hills. If the waters of these streams could be made use of it would be a great blessing to the people of this district. The works should be of a permanent nature, so that they may continue to be useful long after we are gone. I am sure the staff in the office at Regina have gathered a great deal of valuable information in connection with this area, and I want to make the plea to the minister that the engineers should concentrate on this primary objective until it is much closer to accomplishment than is the case at present. In addition, some of these works which are partly finished could be completed at very small cost, and I think that should be done just as soon as men and material are available. The longer they are left unfinished the greater will be the suffering. This is really one of our very urgent problems.

First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to congratulate the minister and the department on what has been done under the P.F.RA. I know this measure was brought into operation by a previous administration, but it took the present minister to realize the

Supply-Agriculture
possibilities of this area. He knows the country; he recognizes the needs, and if you travel through that country you will realize that he and his department should be given great credit for the way these projects are being developed under this act.
This morning I was very glad to hear the minister place emphasis upon the small projects which are to be undertaken. It is all very well for some hon. members to get up in this committee and advocate the expenditure of considerable sums of money on large projects, but in my opinion what is needed more than anything else is the further development of the small dugout and the small dam both on the farm and on the stream in the southern part of Saskatchewan. These small projects, I believe, best serve the needs of the greatest number of people. As far as the expenditure of money is concerned it does not cost much to build one dugout, but collectively they are of great benefit to the farmers of that country. Many farmers who formerly had to draw water three or four miles have benefited from the construction of these small dugouts and dams.
I should like also to bring to the attention of the minister a project on the Souris river, with which I am sure he is well acquainted. This project has been surveyed and fully covered by his department, and I believe the commissioner at Regina is quite prepared to go ahead with it when the money is available. It will consist of the construction of two or three small dams, which will provide storage for considerable water over a matter of about forty miles of country. The valley of the Souris river is quite wide, and if the pumping method of irrigation were adopted a great many acres of land could be developed for the production of hay and even fruit. I was speaking to the commissioner with regard to this project, and he feels that fruit crops could be developed in that valley just as they are now being developed at the experimental farm at Morden.
I also want to commend the minister upon the work he has done in establishing community pastures in that area. These pastures have served a very useful purpose and are still doing so. Years ago, when the drought was upon us, we had community pastures where we could send our stock, where water was provided, and they filled a great need.
I hope the minister will give consideration to this project along the Souris river. If it is not possible to include it in this year's programme I hope he will be able to include it in the programme for next year.

As has been pointed out by other hon. members, the P.F.RA., as it is
commonly called in the west, was begun primarily as an experiment in the so-called drought area. I want to join other hon. members who have given credit for the work that has been done in this connection.
While some of us may from time to time have offered criticism, in the right places, we are also prepared to give credit where credit is due. I sincerely believe that this so-called experiment, in the drought area has proven successful and is beyond the experimental stage. While we were experimenting with that work, the idea was to be made effective in the smaller field. That was the original plan. I was pleased the other day to hear the minister explain how the Moose Jaw water project had been taken care of by a special vote earmarked for that purpose. 1 think that was handled in the proper way, and I suggest that similar work in the future be undertaken in the same fashion.
While I am prepared to admit that the preliminary work, and even the active administration work and the handling of the larger projects, in all probability can best be done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, I do submit that the larger irrigation projects, those connected with the supplying of water to urban centres such as Moose Jaw and Regina, as has been advocated by the hon. member for Davenport, should be provided for by a special vote, and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act should carry out the work. However, the experimental stage of this work, as I suggest, has passed. I believe we have now reached the time when there might be a renaming of the act, and also a rewriting of it so as to widen its scope. The renaming might easily be done by inserting in place of the word "prairie" the word "Canadian", so that we would have a Canadian farm rehabilitation act.
Having gone through the experimental stage in the west, we now have the advantage of knowing what can be done. The time has-arrived when we should take in all the farming areas in Canada. We might have three separate zones, one for the maritimes, one for central Canada, and one for the western provinces, all working under an administrative head. The other evening the hon. member for Cumberland suggested that there should be a reclaiming of the marsh lands in the maritime provinces. That work could' be taken care of, as well as other necessary work. I had hoped when coming to Ottawa that during the course of the session I would have time to get around to other parts of so-called eastern Canada so as to familiarize myself with the conditions in this section of
