I should like to add a word to what has been said in connection with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. There are seven community pastures in the constituency of Kindersley, which I have the honour to represent. Those pastures aggregate 174,680 acres of submarginal land which has been reclaimed. Nearly all the pastures have been operating for three or four years, and the greater portion of them have been regrassed with tame grasses of various kinds, chiefly crested wheat grass. Those pastures are supporting and feeding over 3,000 head of cattle and 2,000 horses. There are two more pastures ready for construction when we can get the men to build them. Those pastures are rendering service not only locally to Kindersley constituency, but to the whole of Canada.
With the advantage of registered Shorthorn and Hereford sires in developing those strains of cattle on the pastures, buyers from eastern Canada are in a position to select from one to three or four cars of feeder steers in the fall if they care to come to that community. They can go into these pastures and soon get plenty of splendid cattle. In truth those cattle are fairly well ready for the market when they come off the pastures in the fall. There are some feeders who would consider them pretty well warmed up, and in condition that the old country pepole like. The way the present minister has extended this work under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, in connection with pastures, is most commendable.
I have one further word in connection with water. I support what the hon. member for Davenport has said. We have cooperated on this subject before. I believe I have spoken with respect to it on two other occasions in this chamber. The hon. member was on sound

ground in practically everything he said in connection with irrigation along the south Saskatchewan river. I did not agree with him, though, in what he said with respect to the area north to Tramping lake. There is a height of land there which would eliminate it from the area. Most of the country to which the hon. member referred could be covered, more particularly that portion near Saskatoon via Eagle creek. It could be taken care of from there. But Tramping lake would have to be filled from the north, either from the North Saskatchewan river or the Red Deer river. It has been suggested we should not take anything from the North Saskatchewan river. It could be secured from the Red Deer and other sources in the west, utilizing Sullivan lake and Tramping lake to take care of the surplus of water now running away.	.

From the remarks made in connection with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act it would appear that there is unanimity with regard to the merits of the act and its administration by the present minister. With that view everyone in western Canada would agree. Scattered throughout western Canada there are about 19.000 individual dugouts, watering dams and small irrigation projects which have proven a veritable boon to western Canada. It was a real tribute to the minister to hear the hon. member for Humboldt suggest this afternoon that the name of the act should be changed to the Canadian farm rehabilitation act and be administered for the whole of Canada in the same way as it has been administered for western Canada. I am in accord with that suggestion. The matter was considered last year by the reconstruction committee, and in an interim report to the house it was recommended that the provisions of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act be extended to other parts of Canada so that districts which might be afflicted would be able to receive the benefits of this legislation.
I concur in the plans that are being developed for the irrigation of certain parts of western Canada. In this connection I would commend the efforts and vision of the director, Mr. Spence. In giving evidence before the reconstruction committee he formulated plans for an irrigation project which would provide water for very extensive areas and assure abundant crops.	_
These amounts are contained in a general vote, but, as has been mentioned by the minister, special votes have been provided for water conservation. This was the case in connection with Saskatoon and later for Moose Jaw and more recently for the town of Hum-

Supply-Agriculture
boldt. In this connection the department has undertaken a search for water to supply this town. I commend the minister for this undertaking. Having recently spent three weeks in Humboldt I know something about the quality of the water there. I think I can say there is not a town in western Canada in greater need of a supply of consumable water.
Mention has been made on more than one occasion of the projects to provide Moose Jaw and Regina with permanent water supplies. It is part of the plan that this water should come from the Saskatchewan river and be piped to these areas. This plan is not new; it was first broached in 1913 when a vote of the burgesses of Moose Jaw, Regina, Weybura and some of the intervening areas, together with the inhabitants of the rural areas concerned, was taken. The proposal was that the city should pay a certain portion of the cost, the provincial government a proportion, while the lands bordering upon the project and which would be benefited therefrom would be taxed. The project was defeated, and until recently there has been little done or said with respect thereto.	*
I would point out that the minister has partly developed this plan by means of an open ditch and pumping station at Riverhurst in order to make available a supply of water for Moose Jaw. Moose Jaw has an acute water situation, and those of us who live in Regina are in sympathy with the situation in which that city finds itself. We are heartily in accord with any plan that may be formulated for the correction of that situation. When the plan was first broached some three or four years ago our citizen body was glad to lend its support to carrying it out.
Regina is not in exactly the same position. Regina is peculiarly situated in a saucer, and it obtains its water supply from a series of artesian wells. These were first drilled some forty years ago and at the present time there are forty-two wells in operation. Water has never been rationed in Regina and there has never been any shortage for domestic purposes. We have an abundance of water to satisfy any reasonable demands of industrial life. The water consumption in Regina for the first six months of this year was 869,000,000 gallons, an average of slightly under 5,000,000 per day or 80 gallons per person. These figures indicate that there is immediately available a supply of water for all reasonable purposes. Within the last few weeks another well has been brought into production with a flow of 1,000,000 gallons per day, and two other wells are being drilled at the present time. Water is found at a depth of from 150 to 180 feet. In addition
to the forty-two wells I have mentioned, certain industries, including two breweries, have artesian wells on their own properties. The General Motors plant have an artesian well, the two packing plants have wells, as has Imperial Oil. It will be apparent that there is available an immediate supply of water.
I want at this juncture to pay a tribute to the hon. member for Davenport for his continued interest in western Canada and in the development of water and irrigation projects in particular. He has had a continued interest in the cities of Regina and Moose Jaw. On several occasions the hon. member has said that he is a retired eastern manufacturer, but unlike other eastern manufacturers the hon. gentleman spends much of his time and considerable of his money in visiting western Canada to ascertain for himself the problems facing that part of the country. I want also to commend him for his industry in eastern Canada. On numerous occasions when addressing eastern audiences the hon. member has emphasized the necessity of the development of western Canada to ensure a prosperous east.
The other evening the hon. member stated that having been engaged in the manufacture of radiators, if he were to establish a plant in Regina the first thing he would ask for would be the water supply. With an inadequate water supply he would be deterred from starting his plant there. I know the extent to which the words of the hon. gentleman are weighed and considered by those in eastern Canada and I hope therefore that eastern manufacturers will not consider that Regina is a continuing victim of the drought and that a shortage of water is a reasonable excuse for their refusal to establish manufacturing plants there.
I should have stated earlier that the city engineers informed me that there had been no appreciable diminution in the supply of water, nor had the water level dropped in the artesian wells in the drought years between 1930-39. I have before me a telegram from the mayor of Regina in which, after expressing his thanks and appreciation to the hon, member for Davenport, and commending the Moose Jaw water project as a post-war undertaking, he says:
Mr. Farrell, waterworks superintendent, quite interested. States present supply adequate with no suggestion of failure but ultimately water from Riverhurst logical.
My view that eastern manufacturers, in addition to the hon. member for Davenport, have some such thought in their minds is confirmed by certain statements made by the hon. member for Danforth, who, before the reconstruc-

Supply-Agriculture
tion committee, said that 'western Canada could not expect industrial development until the water situation in western Canada had been corrected. I am very much afraid that our eastern industrialists are looking for an excuse to keep out of western Canada, rather than to go in there and develop a market. I am constrained to that viewpoint because at the city of Calgary, for example, they have the Bow River and an unlimited supply of excellent water. The same is true of the city of Edmonton, on the north Saskatchewan. The same is true of Battleford in the province of Saskatchewan, where they have the Battle and North Saskatchewan rivers. It is equally true of the city of Saskatoon, where the river flows right through the middle of the city. It is equally true of the city of Prince Albert, where the North Saskatchewan flows right through the city.

The hon. member is speaking
of industrial development on the prairies. I agree with him that that is very desirable, but is it not a fact that electricity can be developed in areas near to coal fields as cheaply by coal as it can be by water, so that there is no reason why the prairies should be denied industrial plants?

That opens up a very
interesting question and one that has been under consideration in our province for many years. In southern Saskatchewan we have some twenty million tons of lignite coal, with an overburden of from 35 to 150 feet. That coal is mined by the strip method. There is a small power plant located down there now that should be utilized and will be utilized at some time in the very near future to a greater extent than at present for the development of electrical energy. I am not so sure that power can be developed from coal as cheaply as it can be from hydro.
But to continue, the city of Brandon likewise is on the banks of the Assiniboine river, and the city of Winnipeg is located at the confluence of the Red and Assiniboine rivers. Therefore we have a superabundance of water in western Canada, but industry has not located in western Canada to the degree that it should have. As an example there is in the city of Calgary a rolling mill. It was estab-Pshed some years ago, but never turned a wheel. It required a superhuman effort on the part of the hon member for Calgary West to keep that rolling mill from being rolled clean out of the province of Alberta about two years ago. Again, there is a steel and iron works in the town of Selkirk in the province of Manitoba which has not operated to the degree that it should have.

No, sir, I am constrained to the viewpoint that it is not water that is the deterrent. It is not a lack of water in the west that compels the centralization of industry in other parts of Canada. We have attempted to establish industry in the west. In my own experience since coming to the city of Regina we have had a soap factory there, a plant for the manufacture of shoes, a tannery, a plant for the manufacture of cigars, a plant for the manufacture of hats, and other establishments of one kind and another. All these plants have folded up and gone out of business. In some cases it was for lack of capital; in other cases it was poor management; but for the most part it was unfair competition from established industry in other parts of Canada that drove them out. Now that must be corrected if we are going to have a better balanced economy in our province. I could give you a great many instances of how it has worked out in western Canada.
While the minister may not think that this is identified with P.F.R.A., I should like to continue for a moment to establish that it is not the shortage of water but some other reasons that deter industry from establishing in western Canada.

Since the hon. member has raised the point I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I hope we shall not get into a discussion of industry under the P.F.R.A. vote because I am hopeful of getting through some time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not want to curtail the discussion but I think the point of order is well taken. The subject is the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

I bow to your judgment, Mr. Chairman, and will make only one other short statement which can be linked up and identified with water and which serves to emphasize the point I want to make.
Some few years ago enterprising farmers north of Regina sunk a well to the depth of 3,300 feet. They got salt water at that depth. In order that their efforts should not be completely abortive, they put in a pumping plant and a drying plant and were ready to put salt on the market. But the day that they were prepared to put salt on the market, the price of salt in the Regina freight area was dropped by $9 per ton. That put that salt project out of business and it has never functioned since.
The C.P.R.

Nff, he said it was the price, not the freight rate that dropped.

Supply-Agriculture

It was not the freight rate but the salt price which dropped in the Regina freight area by $9 per ton. This project was unable to met that competition and has never functioned since.
The hon. member for Davenport suggested a fire hazard existed in our city and that it would be a deterrent to the location of industry there. I believe I have established to his satisfaction that there is a supply of water immediately available to meet any emergency and every contingency ; and I would not have him overlook the artificial lake we have almost in the centre of the city which covers some sixty acres and could be used in case of emergency as an auxiliary.

I should like to endorse particularly the latter part of the remarks made by the hon. member for Regina City. I do not intend to enter into any discussion of the matter of industries; I realize that it does not come up strictly under this item. But in addition to the remarks made by the hon. member, I am sorry to have to say that in certain instances the administration or their officials have discouraged the setting up of industries in western Canada. I refer particularly to flax processing; I know definitely- that it has been discouraged in Saskatchewan, whereas it has been encouraged in Ontario by officials of the government.
I endorse the suggestions which were made this afternoon with respect to -the enlargement of the schemes which the government has been undertaking during the last number of years under the provisions of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I especially endorse the suggestion of the hon. member for Davenport with respect to irrigation. This matter first arose a few years ago when we found ourselves in a straitened situation through drought. Now that conditions have returned more or less to normal I am afraid that many people will forget what occurred at that time, and it is possible-we hope not-that there will be a recurrence of drought conditions and we shall not be properly prepared to meet them. If seems to me that we should be thinking very seriously now of extending as largely as we can irrigation projects which have been carefully worked out and will produce the greatest results. The minister has often described in this chamber that great Palliser triangle which takes in my constituency and a large part of central Saskatchewan, where one needs a certain amount of moisture, but just a certain amount, to produce the best grains in the world. Unfortunately if you do not get that amount you have a crop failure; if you have too much you do not get quite the results you should have in grade and quality. Because of
our scientific researches and our modern knowledge of agricultural produce, excess moisture is not as great a hazard as it used to be. But certainly we should have some protection for the times when the supply of moisture is not sufficient to induce germination and to produce crops in this particular area. Besides, if these vast irrigation schemes were put into effect we would be able to achieve a diversification of agricultural production; in addition to producing very hard wheat we would profit by that diversified economy which, I am sure, all hon. members feel is essential to all parts of Canada.

I should like to make a short contribution from the Ontario standpoint. I am inclined to endorse the standpoint of the hon. member for Humboldt, that P.F.R.A. should be given national application and extended to other parts of the dominion. Even in Ontario we have conditions wherein public assistance might serve a national interest, through the reforestation of certain lands which should never have gone into agricultural production. It seems to me that there is a field for expansion in that direction. At the same time I do not believe that large investments of taxpayers' money should be made in schemes of this kind without the prospect of an ample return for the money expended. I do not know whether I am clear about this scheme

whether at the present time there is a return of any kind. I was led to believe that it was intended that there should be, in course of time. It is true that if you can increase production, the government receives indirectly as a consequence a certain amount of revenue. But in the United States, on schemes such as that by which the reconstruction finance corporation built Boulder dam and many other projects, assessments are made in respect of the services rendered, upon those who benefit by them, and up to the present time the return upon the original capital expenditures has been as much as twenty-five per cent. I do not believe that governments should throw their taxpayers' money around without a prospect of return, and I urge that this principle be kept in mind.
I was out in Saskatchewan in 1937. It was a fairly dry year, and I was much impressed by the necessity of doing something to maintain the families in the drought areas of the west. Any of us who happened to see what conditions were there could only welcome an opportunity of contributing money to the general welfare and well-being of the prairie provinces. But conditions have somewhat changed. Although this year we are asked to vote only two million dollars, I would remind hon. members that there has been a consider-

Supply-Agriculture
able expenditure in the west in these various schemes. I happen to have in my hand a return from the Canadian federal farm loan board, and I find that there is a measure of prosperity even in Saskatchewan, as indicated by the fact that in the year ended March 31 last, of eight million dollars borrowed from the board, two million dollars was paid in the retirement of principal. In other words, in one year of prosperity Saskatchewan farmers have been able to repay one-fourth of their indebtedness to the board. We are very glad that that has taken place, but it seems to me that the time has come when an assessment might be levied on those who derive the benefits from these schemes. In this way capital would be returned and could be reinvested in a kind of revolving fund and the work extended all through the dominion.
I have mentioned this because it seems to me that there is a tendency for us, even in prosperous times, to endeavour to satisfy some desire at the public expense without the prospect of return to the treasury. I hope that when this work is continued, this aspect of the scheme will be given some consideration, so that the money will be returned and made available by way of a revolving fund for expenditures throughout the country.

I shall not attempt to follow all the way through the remarks of the hon. member for Regina city. I was impressed by the able presentation he made. I wish to say a few words to endorse all that he said and more with regard to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act expenditures. No ^ one living in other than the prairies can begin to visualize what those dugouts have meant to the farmers of the west. They have simply transformed large sections of western Canada; and drive where you will to-day you will see splendid herds of cattle from which the owners are reaping good returns, where a few years ago, because of lack of water, they were not able to keep more than two or three cows. During the last few years this has been of particular advantage in supplying food to our allies. I feel sure I am speaking for the general public throughout the west when I say that the Minister of Agriculture, his staff and his engineers, are entitled to a large measure of gratitude and appreciation for the way they have stood by this work. I am speaking of what I have seen, speaking of what I know.	_
Just a few days ago I received a letter from a progressive farmer in Manitoba who fives in a district where water has never been plentiful. He has made considerable money because of those dugouts, and he expresses the hope that in part of that district there will soon be a 
hundred more dugouts placed. I understand the great trouble is the lack of machinery.
I am glad that there is no reduction in the estimates this year for that purpose. I do not regard this as an expenditure; it is an investment. It is an investment that yields rich dividends. These dividends are not payable to western Canada alone; in very large measure they seep back to the east. They mean abundance of business. They mean more and more to the workers of eastern Canada. They tend to the upbuilding of Canada as a whole; and I wish to express my appreciation of the fact that again this year that expenditure or investment, as one may wish to call it, is to be continued.

May I give a word of information to the hon. member for Brant, which I should have given before. These community pastures are now all self-supporting. In fact the sinking fund will more than rebuild the pastures in twenty years.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, what has this to do with the'item before the Chair?

It has to do with prairie farm rehabilitation, and has been incorporated in the book dealing with this subject issued by the minister. During those years the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was set up under the Bennett administration, and has been carried on and extended under the present administration. The hon. member for Brant asked whether or not it pays a return. I join in the suggestion made this afternoon by the hon. member for Humboldt and supported by the hon. member for Regina City- who also advised us that this scheme had been suggested by the committee on rehabilitation as a post-war measure-that the P.F.R.A. be extended as a dominion measure; and experience has shown that it will pay returns. It has brought results. It has paid returns far beyond the extent of the expenditure made under it, in the new hope and determination it has given the people of western Canada, who never could have carried on in recent years if this scheme had not been inaugurated.
In passing let me say this. We often hear the suggestion advanced that people in eastern Canada do not appreciate the needs and difficulties of the people on the prairies. My answer is that we in western Canada can never adequately show our appreciation of the attitude taken by the people of the east dining those dark and difficult days. We may fail to express that appreciation and to pay our tribute of thanks, but the west know that they helped us during our difficult days, and the suggestion advanced this afternoon that the operation of P.F.R.A. be extended to apply^ to all of the country offers just one way in which we, having passed through the experimental stage under this act, may do our bit to assist in the rehabilitation of other parts of Canada. I believe the minister dealt with this matter last year, and I am sure he believes that something along this line must be developed in eastern Canada.
I also dealt with it this morning, just before lunch.

I heard the hon. gentleman deal with it last year; I was not present this morning at the sitting of the
Supply-Agriculture

committee of the whole. I am not in agreement with the suggestion that there should be an expenditure of $100,000,000. To-day I am afraid too many hon. members are apt to recommend the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars without considering the fact that such tremendous expenditures will necessitate increases in taxation. I do feel that a step can be taken in the direction of extending its operation to the whole of Canada without spending anything like the amount mentioned.
I know something of the conditions that exist in Nova Scotia, in the marsh areas referred to not long ago by the hon. member for Cumberland. I feel that this act should be made applicable to projects in all parts of Canada, and that this could be done without difficulty, and certainly without criticism, _ so that something in the way of rehabilitation might be accomplished in the marsh areas of the maritimes.
I join in the very generous tribute that was paid by the hon. member for Regina City to the hon. member for Davenport. I believe that western Canada, regardless of party affiliations, owes a debt of gratitude to this hon. gentleman for what he has done in endeavouring to show the people of this country from his first-hand experience and knowledge something of what unity means in building up a nation, each part dependent upon the other, in order to assure the economic welfare of the whole. That has been the crusade in which the hon. member for Davenport has been engaged for a number of years, and the people of western Canada appreciate what he has done. He has also shown the people of the east something that the hon. member for Brant has lost sight of, which is that in restoring prosperity in western Canada, or in the maritimes, or on the far western slopes of the Pacific, prosperity is brought to those portions of Canada that depend upon industry. That has been the purpose of the work of the hon. member for Davenport, and this being the first opportunity I have had to say a word of commendation, I am glad to be able to do so.
I should like to know from the minister what is being done in connection with the submarginal lands. I know of the work that is being carried on by the land utilization branch, but I have noted that in recent months there has been a gradual return of people to these areas because of the fact that in other parts of the province farm land is difficult to secure and prices have increased. They are returning to these areas which history and experience since 1860 have shown have experienced periods of drought that have

continued from five to seven or even ten years at a time, they being located within the northern confines of the great American desert.

During the years this act has been in operation we have taken
1,268.000	acres of land out of cultivation and put it under pasture. When I say "out of cultivation" I do not mean that all the land had been put under the plough. Some of it, of course, had been included in farms, and the proportion of a farm which is under natural grass in submarginal areas is perhaps greater than in the better areas. We have taken over the land previously operated by individuals, in some cases as farms and in other cases as ranches, under lease from the government, and have placed that many acres under pasture. In the beginning we had a very definite opinion in that regard. It will be recalled that- this method of dealing with submarginal lands was not contained in the act as it was first drafted but was added in one of the amendments made in 1936 or 1937, shortly after I took over the department. When we began to deal with the matter we asked the provinces, since the lands had been returned to them, to turn over to us any of these lands over which they had control. We asked them to turn over to the federal government, through the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and through the Department of Agriculture, any of the lands they desired us to put into pasture. Only one province agreed to do that. Saskatchewan agreed to turn the lands over and place them under the ownership of the federal government, if they were fenced and put into pasture.
The reason we were insisting upon that at the beginning was that we wished to prevent for all time farmers going back on those lands. And so we wanted them to be under the ownership of the federal government. We put fences around them, and we make them available to the people in the community. In obtaining that control and ownership of the lands we agreed to enter into some kind of arrangement with any individuals on the lands to provide for moving them off and putting them on better lands. We preferred to put them on lands outside the pastures, where they could get a better grade of land, and at the same time utilize the pasture in order to assist them in carrying on. But in addition to that we did provide to move them. This has a very important bearing on the item we are going to discuss next, namely that having to do with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

Many persons have made representations to me to the effect that we should enlarge the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to take in every individual on an individual basis. The reason we did not do that from the beginning, was that under this act we have provided for financing an individual when moving off submarginal lands. We did not wish, under another act, to finance his staying there. In other words if you have four or five individuals in the middle of a township, where everyone else is getting by under the same weather conditions, it would appear to us that to assist that small group of individuals to remain in the area would mean that we would be assisting people, in many instances, to remain on su.bmarginal lands. And so we suggest that the assistance we ought to give to that type of individual is assistance to him to move away from there and to go on better lands. We applied that principle under this act, and we have moved a great many people out of Saskatchewan, or off some lands in Saskatchewan, to other lands. I can look up the exact figures if they are required.
About how many?

I think that will be
found in the report the hon. member has in his hand. My memory is that we moved about a thousand families. We are carrying on on that basis in Saskatchewan.
In Alberta we have agreed to enter into an arrangement under which we have control of the lands over a twenty-year period. But up to date the Alberta government has not signed that arrangement. For that reason we have not been able to form what are known as community pastures in that province. In Manitoba, where the situation is not quite the same, there are very few of these areas upon which people are located that could be organized into pastures, and where there is any considerable amount of government-owned land. We have there entered into arrangements under which we have assisted in organizing very much smaller pastures than are found in Saskatchewan. Most of those have been taken over for operation by the municipalities. That is, we have not taken actual ownership of the lands. We have taken some control for a period of time, and, having made capital expenditures, in some cases we have turned the administration back to the municipalities for purposes of operation.
We have different methods in the different places in which we are operating. Our general desire is to get people off the submarginal lands. There is legislation in each of the provinces dealing with submarginal lands. In Saskatchewan, under certain legislation in
that province, they designate certain lands as submarginal. We deal with those lands on the basis upon which they have been designated. In other words, it must be a matter of cooperation between the federal and provincial governments, when lands are under the control of the province. But the basic principle underlying our desire is that if we are going to take land and fence it into large pastures, we build fences which will be good for at least twenty years, we put grass on those lands, and also supply breeding stock. We put sires in the pastures so that there will be good stock. We ought to have ownership of those lands to prevent someone from coming back when prices are high and conditions particularly good and starting in on those farms again. We wished to make resettlement permanent.
As to the other suggestion, I doubt very much if the hon. member for Lake Centre can quote me at any time as having said anything different from what he has just read from the report. I have never been one who believed that the depression in Canada was or could have been caused by any government in this country. That is one reason I am not in favour of the C.C.F. policy. I do not think it can be corrected inside this country. I think when we talk about the depression which existed in the thirties as being something which we ourselves could correct, without any consideration being given at all to what happened outside of Canada, we are approaching it from an entirely wrong angle. I still think the w'ay our problem can be solved here is by having conditions both inside and outside Canada under which we are prepared to exchange our products very freely. That of course depends upon our being able to find markets somewhere else for the products we produce here in surplus quantities. When we are not able to do that, as we were not during the time referred to, difficulties arise. I think it is in the report to which reference has been made that one of the causes of our not being able to do that was that restrictions were placed upon the shipments of our products into other countries, as a result of the desire to increase the production of the same products in those countries.
Mr. IiUHL: What about the home market?

My friends over there would like to force 560,000,000 bushels of wheat and 800,000,000 pounds of bacon and ham down the throats cf 12,000,000 people, and it just cannot be done. We have to be able to find other people who are prepared to eat some of it. That of course is what we desire to do under those circumstances.

All this, however, is aside from the matter now under discussion. The position is that under rehabilitation we are attempting to get submarginal lands out of cultivation, and making a further attempt to keep them out. We must have a certain amount of cooperation both from provincial governments and from individuals on the lands, if that is to be accomplished. In some cases we require the cooperation of municipal councils. I must say that in a very large degree we have had cooperation from all those sources. Because of that cooperation we have been able to accomplish something in connection with the rehabilitation of that country.
Has the department any scheme for the use of submarginal lands other than the establishment of pastures and reseeding in grasses?

There are some lands which would be considered submarginal in relation to the growing of wheat, let us say, which would not be submarginal in relation to the growing of other crops. The best illustration of that, one which would be best understood by hon. members in all parts of the house and from all parts of Canada, would be that area in which tobacco is grown to a very considerable extent in southwestern Ontario. There is a section there which at one time would have been classed as submarginal, and to-day it is perhaps the most valuable land in Canada because they are able to grow tobacco on it. There are other lands elsewhere of the same character. I know of a farm in Saskatchewan, a quarter-section, which was homesteaded by a man who went almost bankrupt. I do not know whether he came from Prince Edward Island or one of the other maritimes, but in any case he knew how to grow potatoes. He put in about fifteen or twenty acres of potatoes on this farm, which was located about fifty miles from Regina. Within a very few years he was able not only to get out of bankruptcy but to retire in Regina, and he has lived there ever since. That land would be considered as submarginal if you were going to grow wheat on it, but it could grow another product and make considerable money for the owner.
I realize there is another factor involved in this. If all the land of that type in Saskatchewan were put into potatoes, everyone would go broke trying to grow potatoes. A few individuals can become fairly wealthy producing a product as long as too many do not go into the production. There are many things involved in grading land as submarginal. The location is one-where it is in relation to a

city or in relation to some other market. However, generally speaking, submarginal land is that light, sandy land found in many sections of the country, or land that is so polluted with alkali that it is not suitable for the growing of ordinary crops.

I should like to ask a question based on an application by the town of Lumsden requesting certain expenditures from this vote for repairs of a dike. I do not often bring up individual cases, but this seems to be a proper one having regard to the changes that were made at Craven in connection with the Long lake development. I should like a report from the minister as to what has been done in connection with the request made by that town.

I am not in a position to deal with the exact request that was made, but I know some of the circumstances. This morning I think I mentioned the fact that water flows into Long lake early in the season and fills it up, and some years it flows out again after it has reached a certain level. There have been times when Lumsden has been flooded. We hope to be able to control that situation to a certain extent by keeping water back in Buffalo lake, further west, and letting it come down later on in the year. We have built a dike across the south end of Long lake and in that dike we have placed a cement structure to control the water flowing in and out. Not everyone
agrees with what the engineers hope will happen in connection with that work. As a matter of fact we have found obstructions there, probably not the dam but rather the silting up of the ditch which runs from the Qu'Appelle river into Long lake, and which has been there for a long time. The water does not flow in through the old, original, natural creek; it flows through a ditch dug many years ago, and we put in a cement structure to control it. Some people think the engineers did not put the bottom of that structure down low enough, and that as a result it has something to do with obstructing the water getting in. In order to satisfy them, I think it was last spring we opened a certain part of that dike to let in more water, in order to raise the level of the lake much higher than it would otherwise have been.
I am not certain as to what has happened since that time, whether they are replacing the dike or widening the opening still further, or just what they are doing. However, the engineers are reporting continuously on the matter and some work is being done, although I am not clear as to just what it is.

I appreciate the work that has been done on the south side of the lake, and understand generally the plan the engineers are following. What I had in mind particularly was the request of the town of Lumsden.
Have you the request there, and, if so, would you read it?

The matter has been brought up on two or three occasions, and an application was made directly to the Regina district office. The request is that the department bear a share of the cost of repairs to the dike on the south side of the Qu'Appelle river where it passes through Lumsden. When the dike was constructed in 1929 the federal Department of Public Works bore seventy-five per cent of the cost. The dike was constructed of earth, and a section beginning near Lake street and extending a short distance on James street was constructed of planking bolted to piling. It was thought this would last for a considerable length of time; I believe the estimate was twenty years, but as a result of the change in the flow of water consequent upon the development work which took place last year, damage occurred thereto. The result is that the dike became in dangerous condition. The request is that the town should not be held responsible for the repairs to this dike when those repairs are made necessary by the changes which have taken place in the engineering

Then they went through and made another survey; the chief inspector, I believe it was Mr. Scott, was sent out. My information is to the effect that his report showed that production for that township was less than eight bushels per acre. The producers in that area have been doing their very best to get fair play under the existing set-up, but in spite of the fact that the chief inspector's report showed that they came within the bonus area, they have been told that they do not qualify. Is there any way whereby further appeals can be made; what tribunal can they apply to for a further consideration of their plea? The producers have gone about this matter methodically. They have done considerable work themselves by way of making surveys, and they feel they have been discriminated against. What can be done?

The practice followed is that inspectors go out and make inspections. If there is no question that they are under eight bushels, it is passed, But in cases where there is any question, they all go to the board. This is a board of three members, the chairman of which is Professor MacEwen of Saskatchewan agricultural college. Then there is Mr. Stevenson, who is here at the table with me. The third representative is really named by the Department of Finance, and at the present time is Mr. Holmes of Saskatoon.
Those three men are the board, and1 all questionable cases are referred to them. They are the board to whom final appeal is made; there is on appeal beyond them. In this particular case, however, as has been said there

Supply-Agriculture
have been two inspections. One of them was made in the summer months and the other in February. One can understand why it is much more difficult to make a proper inspection in February than it is in the summer, at the time the crop is growing.
In, some respects, yes.

Yes, in some respects. The second report made would indicate, if one takes the figures obtained at that time, that it would be slightly under eight bushels. The other figure, which was taken when they thought all the facts were available, showed over eight bushels. This matter has been before the board1 three times, and each time the board has refused to pass it. There is only one way whereby any recourse can be had. The board has final authority, and the only action that can be taken is to have the matter reconsidered by the board. That is all that can be done.
Were all members of the board present in each of the three reviews?
The second time only two were present, but I understand they were all present the last time. The two western members considered it the first time.

Nothing further can
be done; that would be the position?
Nothing more than make an appeal to the board, and I do not imagine, after the board have considered it three times, they would be very anxious to consider it again.

I should like to ask a question with respect to the regulations governing rectangular plots within a township accepted for benefits under this act. I know the government has made the regulation with a view to taking in certain areas in a township, where perhaps the whole township may not get the average crop required to meet the conditions in the regulations. I think that was a good move, but it does complicate matters to some extent.
I shall explain to the minister what I mean.
I have in mind a case where all the sections coming down the side of one township are not in a position to receive benefits from the drought bonus. All the other sections in the township, because that particular block went below the average, receive the benefit' of the bonus.
The condition which has arisen is this. One man whose property is in a section bordering on the block that gets the benefits had only six and a half bushels to the acre in the last

year's crop. However, his neighbour, who is within the block which receives the benefit, had an average crop greater than did this man iu question. I can understand the government's policy, with respect to their not being able to deal with every case on its individual merits, but one can hardly explain that to a farmer who finds that his neighbour gets a higher average on his crop.
Is that a wheat crop?

Yes, a wheat crop. The one man receives the benefits of the bonus, while the other, who has a smaller crop than his neighbour, is ruled out because he does not come within the specified rectangular block. Could the minister change the regulations in some way so that that peculiarity would not exist? I believe that the minister would agree it is unfair, and that the regulations should be changed to meet circumstances of that kind.

Before the minister replies I should like to place on record a similar example. Before doing so, however, I would say that while listening to the minister's explanation I noted that he made the remark, when another item was under discussion, that we were paying money to some people to get them out of submarginal areas, and that consequently it was not deemed advisable to pay them money to remain on submarginal lands. I appreciate that explanation, and it covers the situation very nicely. Yet at the same time it does not cover problems such as described by the hon. member for Macleod, nor does it cover problems such as I shall now draw to the minister's attention. In the past I have noticed a number of similar cases.
In township 37, range 24, in the municipality in which I live, they had a low yield; yet that township cannot be considered submarginal land. Over a period of years they had produced in that township very good crops. This year, with the exception of about two sections in one corner of the township, they had poor crops. In that corner they had one or two fairly heavy showers. The farmers in that corner of the township were not better farmers than those in the remainder, but the showers had helped them out. It was found at a later time that the township was slightly over eight bushels to the acre. The question still remains in the minds of many people in that township as to whether the actual returns from those two sections were as large as had been reported.
Leaving that aside, however, the fact is that the yield in the rest of the township was away below eight bushels to the acre. What these people wanted to do was to have the remainder of the township, less those two sections, blocked
Supply-Agriculture

over to an area which was already entitled to receive assistance. They were informed, however, that that could not be done. I believe that about one-third of the township west of this area was permitted to block itself with the township lying to the south. That is, they were in range 25. It was township 36 which was entitled to receive the assistance, and the department allowed township 37, range 25, to block a certain area over to 36. But when the people of township 37, range 24, wanted to block their territory over to another township they were told that, under the act, that could not be done.
It is difficult for people to understand why they cannot receive any benefit from this plan, simply because one comer of the township happens to be a few bushels over. They do not understand how this plan is going to help them, and other townships which have been paying into the fund right along. Then, when they see their neighbouring township blocked in with another township receiving assistance, they cannot understand why they are refused that assistance. I wrote to the minister about this case, but both he and I have been on a rather long journey since. I have not received any reply and I was just wondering whether he got my letter.

The reason why I have not replied is that I have made a test case out of this one and have submitted it to the justice department. They gave me one reply, but I was not satisfied with it and I sent the case back to them. I did not want to reply to the hon. member until I was sure of what I was talking about. We said that if a block of townships or even one township were already under the act and there were at least nine sections which were lying alongside and which were rectangular in shape that could qualify, they could be declared in. That is what happened in connection with this township. It was taken in and we took in nine or more sections of the next township.
The other group of sections the hon. member is speaking about were over in the next range. I am not a lawyer and I certainly am not a constitutional lawyer. According to the act the minister is to make the payments, although they are made according to the method we have been discussing here. However, the act states that the minister has authority to make payments. The only way I can make payments under the wording of the act is to make them to those townships where it is admitted that payments can be made.
I contend that I am only able to make payments in a township such as that even when only part of it is considered as being in, if it
(Mr. Burton.]
is declared a township. I contend also that the other township lying alongside should be able to get in because it is alongside one declared in. If I am right, the act will not need any amendment in order to get the decision desired here. If I am wrong, the act will require some amendment in order to have that decision given. I am not in position now to make a reply, but I hope to be in a short time.
The other question raised by the hon. member for Macleod is one that has been before us ever since the act was first drawn. It would not make any difference whether such a farm was on one of those borderlines, that is between a township and the adjoining nine sections, on the borderline of a township that is in and a township that is completely out. You will find farmers on one side of the road who have yields under eight bushels to the acre, and farmers on the other side whose yields are above eight bushels to the acre. But there is one thing that we should not lose sight of. We are not paying on wheat. This has nothing to do with wheat as such. We simply use wheat as a barometer to find out what the weather is like in a particular district.
A farmer on one side of the road may have wheat that runs twenty bushels to the acre, while a farmer on the other side may be getting only five bushels to the acre. This may be due entirely to the fact that one man's wheat was on spring ploughing, while he had put his coarse grains on summer-fallow, whereas the man across the road put his wheat on summer-fallow. If you are going to determine whether or not both men are in exactly the same position you would have to take a complete record of everything that had been produced on the farms; you would require to have a complete record of the operations of both men in live stock, coarse grains, vegetables, poultry and everything else.
We took the simpler way. We decided to take a township and allow nine sections in on the border, or take away nine sections in order to get away from any zigzagging lines. It is impossible to determine just because one man had six bushels to the acre and another had four, that one should be in and the other should be out. We have to draw a line somewhere, and no matter how you attempted to draw it you would run into difficulty. You could not have lines running angleways across a man's farm; you have to go up one side and down the other. No matter how you drew the line you would always have some farmers outside who had a lower yield of wheat. However, when you got a few miles away that would be corrected by the fact that they all would have more.

I expect that I shall have to accept the minister's statement. I agree, of course, that it presents quite a problem, but I suggest that if there is a section or a farm, or whatever size the piece of land may be, that borders upon the nine sections or whatever the rectangular may be, it should receive the benefits provided that the yield is below the minimum. I make that suggestion to the minister and hope that he will take it into consideration. It would not be so bad if all those in the township who were receiving benefits averaged less than the man, who was not receiving benefits, but in some cases they average more. I ask the minister to consider my suggestion.

I find that most people appreciate this legislation; they find it of great help and they want to see it kept going. However, I also find that a lot of bitterness exists for the reasons that have been mentioned. One man with a yield of nine or ten bushels will be getting the bonus and another fellow with a yield of six, five or even, four bushels to the acre cannot get the bonus. I realize that this is not an insurance scheme. If it were, it would be under the province and the premium would be much higher.
I should like to suggest to the minister once more the possibility of having each individual investigated. I know it would be an impossible task to have a special man go out to each farmer in the area, but I was wondering if it would not be possible to get the information from the municipal councils. They usually know the yields. Then investigation could be made of those who were reported by the municipal councils. I have found it impossible to answer a man who says, "Why should I not get the bonus when I have a complete crop failure when some other man with a much larger yield is able to get it?" I am wondering if the minister will not consider this suggestion. I am sure he has considered it already.
'Mr. QUELCH: Most of the complaints I get are similar to those which have been enumerated by other hon. members. However, there is another group of farmers who are always penalized under this act. I am referring to the farmer with fairly poor land who lives in a township where the majority of the land is good. Even though such a man has a crop failure he can get no benefits because the average yield of the township is above twelve bushels to the acre. He suffers because the majority of the land is good while his is poor.
I remember that when this question was raised some years ago the minister suggested that it might be possible to define the areas on the basis of soil classification. He said at that
100-324i
time that the department was investigating the question whether it would be possible to define areas on the basis of soil classification rather than on the township basis. Would the minister say whether anything has been done in that regard.
The greatest difficulty is that you would have to eliminate all submarginal land if we proceeded on the basis *ny hon. friend suggests.
I am not referring to submarginal land but simply to lighter land.

There are different ideas as to submarginal lands. Somebody would have to make up his mind what was to be eliminated. I think the simplest way to eliminate these lands is by the method we are pursuing, to take a block of land and say chat if the majority have good jerops in that area and there are people in that district who cannot get the average yield there is something wrong with the land or something wrong with the man who is farming it. There is the additional fact that men farm in different ways. A man with live stock is more anxious to grow coarse grains than wheat, and he may put his wheat on land that is not quite so well prepared. He may put his wheat on his spring ploughing, and he may put his coarse grains, in a year that was dry, on his summer-fallow in order to make sure that he will have feed grain. The present method makes allowances for all that. I do not see how you could do it in any other way. I have not been able to satisfy myself that any other method would be better.

Another thing that is giving the department a headache is this question of deciding whether a father and son shall be considered as farming one or two units. I have one or two of these cases. I have not been able to understand the basis for some of the decisions that have been made. In two cases that seem identical you will have a decision in the one case that the farms are two units, and in the other case they will be regarded as one unit.
Has the hon. member experienced many of these difficulties within he last two months?
I have two or three cases running around just now.

The reason why I asked the question is this, that the board has been changed because our recent chairman became organizer for one of the political parties, not the Liberal party. He has gone and we now
Supply-Agriculture

have a new chairman. When the new chairman took over, we had a meeting here. I had discovered just before that, that a set of regulations had been drawn up by the old board. They were really interpretations of the regulations and many of them had to do with this father and son question. I took objection to that on the ground that the board were passing regulations that only the governor in council could pass and that the regulations as passed by the governor in council contemplated every case being dealt with separately on its merits. The board was to consider all the facts and. then give its decision, and that is the basis on which the new board has been operating. They have reported to me that they are finding it much more satisfactory to take each case separately and deal with it on its merits, go into all the facts and give their decision. All we have in mind is this, that a person must be debarred from trying to make two collections when there ought to be only one. For instance, a man may have 800 acres under cultivation and he may say: If I run this myself I will get one payment up to 200 acres, but if I divide the farm into two farms of 400 acres each, I shall get the bonus twice on the 200 acres. We are trying to eliminate that kind of case. We want to pay the bonus in a bona fide case because our intention is to encourage fathers to turn over their land to their sons when they reach a certain age, rather than have the son working under the father all his lifetime. That is the basis on which we are now proceeding, and I do not think there will be as much difficulty in the future.

Is there any intention of lowering the age, because boys start farming now at eighteen and in Alberta a young man can vote at nineteen, but here in order to qualify he has to be twenty. I think the age should be lowered to eighteen.
If they do not live with their parents they can qualify at any age. Twenty is the age when they are living at home.
It is in those cases that the iifficulty arises, when the boy is living with ais father. It is hard to decide whether it is two units or one.
We are considering it continuously, and I am glad to say that my views are similar to those of the hon. gentleman.

I appreciate very much the kindness and the valuable assistance which the superintendent of the P.F.A.A. in Edmonton has given to me in the past few years.

There was a time when I criticized the administration rather harshly. That was when the bonuses were first being paid and the organization had not quite found itself. Things were in rather a muddle then. But since they have become organized I find that the department is quite efficient. Naturally I have not been able to get all I wanted, but they have taken an interest in the cases that I have submitted to them, and while I am handing out bouquets I might also say the same for the minister, who has looked into one or two tough cases for me.
I should like to ask a question in regard to the regulation governing payments in the case of a man who operates a farm, part of which is irrigated. The particular case I have in mind is that of a farmer who has fifty acres of irrigated land and another farm some forty or fifty miles away. Because he has fifty acres of irrigated land on one parcel of land, he cannot get any benefits under the act in respect of his farm that is forty or fifty miles away, even though it would qualify. I would not be so persistent if the farmer who has this irrigated property had had a good crop, but one year it was very dry and the weeds did not come up that year. Next year he put in some flax on those fifty acres of irrigated land. The weeds came up and he had a tough time getting a crop of flax at all. He raised only a very small crop. He naturally expected that his other farm was going to help him out. Tlis other farm went below the required average bushels per acre, but because he had this irrigated land he could get no benefits under the act in respect of the other farm. I am sure that the minister will look into this case if I give him the particulars. This cannot be an isolated case; there must be others similar. Could the minister throw some light on a case of that kind?

I am told by a member of the board who is here that cases of that kind have not come here. I am told that there are a few cases of that kind in Alberta. The wording of the regulation is, "farm lands operated by a farmer who as owner or tenant also operates more than fifty acres of land which is part of an irrigated system." It would depend entirely on the interpretation placed on the land operated by the farmer. If a man has an irrigated farm and another farm one hundred miles away, let us say, it would be rather a stretch of the imagination to say it was the same farm. Even if it is forty miles or twenty miles it is the same thing. I think if they were just a mile apart, if a man lives a mile away and operates both places from the same buildings, it would be difficult to give it any other interpretation

Customs Tariff
than the one which is given here. It has not come to my attention on that basis before. I think I had better get a legal opinion on it, and if they adopt that view I would have to have the regulation amended. It is not in the act; it is in the regulations.

These farms are about
fifty miles apart. I can quite understand that if two farms are about a mile or so apart you could use the same equipment on each farm. But this man cannot do that; he cannot haul his equipment every few days about fifty miles. In one letter I received from the department at Edmonton-without mentioning the name of the case-a paragraph reads this way: Mr. So-and-so

-had a tough break with his flax crop. Nevertheless according to (g) of clause 6 of the act we cannot pay him a P.F.A. claim for 1943.
I can quite understand that he cannot have the benefits of the scheme if he is working one farm and another adjacent to it, if he has irrigated land; but a man who does not get very much income from that irrigated land and has a farm which he has to operate separately some considerable distance away should, it seems to me, have the benefits of the act if that distant farm yields only a small average crop.
Send the case to me.
Thank you; I will.

If that is the case the mountain has laboured and brought forth a mouse, so far as the farmer is concerned.

The hon. gentleman may be right. I felt that I should bring this point to the attention of the committee and more particularly to the attention of those hon. gentlemen who believe the removal of this duty will be a great thing for the_farmers. If I could help the farmers I would certainly do so, but $1.25 out of every $1,000 they spend is not a very magnanimous gift. The figures I have given are the latest I have been able to obtain. If any hon. member has been able to get other figures I am sure the committee would be glad to have them. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the removal of this duty will not give the Canadian farmer any greater ability to compete.
What about the worker? If the removal of this duty results in less employment I am afraid the adverse effect on the worker will be much greater than the beneficial effect on the farmer. Farmers are interested in maintaining a healthy home industry, because employment is dependent upon it and employment means an ever-expanding home market for farm products. I believe the farmer is just as much interested as anyone elsfe in having a large home market for his products.
May I also bring to the attention of the committee the fact that all the goods the farmer produces are not on the free list as far as the tariff goes. After listening to discussions in this house one might come to the conclusion that all manufactured goods are protected by high tariffs while farm products have no tariff protection. Let me remind hon. members that a great many farm products have substantial tariff protection. I will not take the time of the committee to mention the duty in each instance, but there is a substantial duty on live cattle, sheep, hogs, 
fresh beef, Iamb, canned meats, baby chicks, bacon and hams, beef in brine, lard, tallow, eggs in shell, cheese, butter, powdered) milk and so on. I am quite confident that if many eggs were brought into this country, or if a great deal of butter came here, the very first people who would rise in their places in this house and demand that something be done would be those representing rural constituencies. So that it is not entirely one-sided; there are tariffs on manufactured goods and tariffs on farm products.
My objection to the removal of this duty at this time, however, is rather to the way in which it is being done. As I said during the budget debate there has been virtual agreement among the united nations, although it has not been put in writing, to reduce tariffs after the war by multilateral agreements. In my opinion at all events it is a mistake to adjust tariffs while the present upset economic conditions prevail throughout the world. It is a mistake to adjust tariffs downward without some compensating advantages from other countries with which we are trading. The best example of that is, I think, to be found in the action taken recently by Canada in connection with cream separators. In the United States they have a tariff against us of 12J per cent on cream separators selling for more than $50. I am not particularly blaming the government in this connection, because apparently the removal of this duty meets with the aproval of all hon. members, and each must accept his share of thg responsibility. If this matter had been handled judiciously by parliament, instead of putting cream separators on the free list we could have arranged a saw-off with the United States, so that if their nationals were to be granted the privilege of shipping cream separators into Canada without the payment of duty, Canadian nationals would have a similar privilege. Under the method which has been adopted, however, we have thrown away our bargaining position in that respect.
What about agricultural implements entering the United States from Canada. What duty is there against them?

I had not intended to
speak at this time, but the remarks of my esteemed friend, a gentleman I have grown to like more each year I have sat in the house, have prompted me to add a word or two. The committee will recall that I asked him a question as to the duty on Canadian farm machinery entering the United States.
I did not hear it.

I asked the hon. member
as to what was the duty on Canadianr-made agricultural implements entering the United States.

I
thought the hon. member was referring to cream separators.
No; the hon. member said that he was talking about cream separators at the time. My impression is that agricultural implements have entered the United States from Canada free of duty for many years.
Not cream separators.
I am talking about agricultural machinery.	_

You cannot cut wheat
with a cream separator.

I should also like to remind the hon. member, and the Liberal party, to which I am an adherent, if nothing more, that implements free of duty, for farming operations, have formed a part of the Liberal platform ever since 1919. After twenty-five years that promise is being redeemed. And yet the hon. member believes it is a step in the wrong direction.
Well, coming from western Canada, being a farmer and having purchased a considerable amount of machinery for farming-and mostly Canadian machinery at that-I feel that this relief is about due. In my view the duty does mean something to the farmers who have to purchase that machinery. I believe that a monopoly exists in regard to farm machinery, and that removing the duty does not mean anything, so far as prices are concerned, unless some other measure is taken.
I think the hon. member said that it costs about three per cent of the farmer's dollar to maintain machinery, and he challenged anyone in the house to offer figures to controvert that statement. All the hon. member has to do is to look into what the government will lend a veteran who goes to take up land. He will be granted $4,800 to purchase the land, and $1,200 to buy the machinery. The purchase price of the machinery amounts to twenty-five per cent of the total loan. I say from experience that if a man wishes to farm now he will pay approximately fifty per cent for farm machinery and fifty per cent for land. It is a fifty-fifty proposition. To start farming now one would have to lay out as much money for machinery as he would for the land.
I was talking about the annual outlay.
Well, of course you cannot farm unless you get started. I am talking about the farmer who wants to get started on the farm, and who will need as much money to equip the farm as to buy the land.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
You know something about farming.
