Well, I am sure if the hon. member for Brantford City does not know as much about farming as I do, he knows far more about most other things.

Oh,
I would not agree with that.

I have .always respected him very much, and I honour him very highly. However, I did not wish to go home to my constituency and tell them that I had sat idly by in the House of Commons while Liberal members, members of the Progressive Conservative party, members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party and members of the Social Credit party had stood up and defended the duties on agricultural machinery. I would not feel that I had done my duty. So that I now rise again to protest against the hon. member's statement that this is a step in the wrong direction. I believe that it is in the right direction, and that it is just overdue by twenty-five years.

The hon. member for Brantford City mentioned that the duty was being taken off cream separators. I quite agree with what he has said. The removal of this duty is going to make a great difference to workers in Canada after the war is over. The duty being taken off cream separators this year will not save the farmers very much, because there are very few cream separators coming into this country from the United States or any other country. After the war is over I am wondering what the workers in one of the largest cream separator plants in the world-the one in Peterborough-are going to do. They will be out of work. Many of those men and women are buying homes to-day. If they are thrown out of jobs through machinery entering Canada ' free of duty, machinery which will be coming into Canada from Sweden and from other countries, they will have a' just grievance. I hope this measure will be taken off the books next year.

The policy of the government respecting customs tariff item 409, which is now before us, was set out in the budget speech by the minister. The principle affecting all these agricultural machinery items is the same. The government to-day does not know where it stands. I know that the agricultural implements industry has been contributing a great part to the war effort. I have seen the plants of the Massey-Harris Company in Toronto, which are busy on war work, almost entirely. There are no implements coming into Canada owing to the war, tariff or no tariff.
Whether this item calls for duty, or does not call for it, the fact remains that the policy of the government at the present time in respect of this and following items is simply one of shadow-boxing and mere window-dressing. That is all it is, and with a war on it means nothing. As hon. members know, the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding dealt with this problem, and adopted a policy of imperial preference. That was followed for some years with our best steady customer, Britain.
Someone may ask what was done at the meeting of Prime Ministers which took place in London, England, in May. We understand that matters of imperial tradte, and trade of all kinds, and affecting all classes of materials, were dealt with at that conference and the future of imperial preferences was discussed. I might add that when the Drury government was in office in Ontario some of the same proposals were made with respect to agricultural implements. While he was premier, Mr. Drury came to Ottawa. At that time he headed a so-called farmer-labour government. What did they do? They came here and they addressed Mr. King's cabinet. Mr. Robb was Minister of Finance. They advanced the same proposals, through a brief of the Canadian council of agriculture, for free trade in agricultural implements and all along the line. They said that protection was an unmitigated evil, that they wanted to get a spade to dig and root it out. Protection for this industry was the policy of all governments in the early days of this country to 1921. What did the present government do when they came into office in 1,921? They did not reduce tariffs all along the line; they did little or nothing to lower tariffs.
Tariff protection has created work and employment. We have a war on now, and this is just some window-dressing instead of doing something for the farmers on the prairies. The best friends the farmers on the prairies have are the people in the east. I believe in the policy of confederation, each for all and all for each. What is for the benefit of one province is for the benefit of them all. There is a war on; we have had the Ogdens-burg agreement and others, and the result of war is that there is very little of this type of agricultural implements being shipped across the border into Canada, and our agricultural industries are converted to other war work accordingly.
What is going to happen to these men in this industry after the war, the men who work at the Massey-Harris plant in Toronto, the plant in Brantford and in many other places?

Customs Tariff
When the war is over what is going to happen to labour because of this policy? Do not overlook the fact that the United States with its population of 130,000,000 had the Hawley-Smoot tariff regarding all of these industries. In the British House of Commons that tariff was called the eighth wonder of the world in high protection. The Republican party may have a majority in congress and their policy as given at Chicago two weeks ago will be to protect their home market all along the line for themselves. Why should not they protect their home market? Why should we not adopt the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding of empire preferences also, as a home-export market? When the war is over, what is to become of the men in this agricultural industry
What has been happening in the other dominions? Mr. Curtin, Mr. Fraser and the other prime ministers have been sounding the same battle cry of empire trade and the empire family first over in London. I believe this matter was discussed in London when our Prime Minister was there. What is to become of the industries like the agricultural industry and hundreds of others? Something should be done about it. Take Russia with its population of 180,000,000 people. Russia is going to look after her own people and her own home markets by high protection. They have already announced a policy along those lines, and Britain has a separate bi-lateral policy with them for twenty years, signed at Moscow.
I was surprised when I looked over the budget to find that the government was all at sea on this empire trade question. The people in the British empire believe in the preference. The British empire has been our best customer and our steady market; it has been the best friend of the prairie provinces. We have been able to sell our products in exchange for goods and services. The imports and exports have created a tremendous amount of work and the farmers of the prairies have been provided with a steady market, not one that is here to-day and gone to-morrow, gone for the cry of internationalism.
The British empire is going into liquidation by default unless we look out and hold to our home market for our family first and any surplus for others. We should take a leaf out of what Russia and the United States are doing in connection with their industries, in safeguarding their own home market. When the war is over, there will always be tariffs. Look at the resolutions which were passed a week ago at Chicago by the Republican party. They are going to go back to the old days when they looked after their own people first, and the same with Russia with her 180,000,000 people, and who can blame them? Great
Britain has lost a quarter of a billion pounds in investments overseas. These have been marketed and put up as a pledge for the war, for munitions and food. She has lost all that and she needs the support of a policy like that adopted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding. They were both Liberals, but they gave Great Britain preference and increased our trade with Britain and that of Britain with Canada.
Is the government going to throw overboard the Ottawa agreements for separate trade agreements? If so, they should announce their policy to Australia and New Zealand, If so, Canada will be sounding the death knell of the British empire unless we have this empire trade and .preference. I believe the prime ministers discussed this whole problem in London. The British empire will go by default and into liquidation unless home markets are available as they have been in the past.
Let me refer to this particular item. I remember when Mr. Drury came here and said that protection was an unmitigated evil. I was in the railway committee room when a large deputation representing the Canadian council of agriculture came here. They attacked the system which had been built up in this country and which had done so much for this country and for the empire. They said it was an unmitigated evil and should be wiped out altogether. Thousands of people left Ontario to go to the United States for jobs, many of them returned soldiers from the last war who had fought at the risk of their lives for this country. We are dealing only with this particular industry, but when the next budget comes down it will sound the deathknell of the automobile industry and many other industries.
I am in complete sympathy with the farmer because I know he has had to pay too much for these implements. When I first entered this house I suggested that the minister should have an expert in his department who would set a fair price on these agricultural implements to be paid by the farmers on the prairies.
This question will have to be solved in the next election. When the war is over there will be tens of thousands of our workers out of work. I remember when ward 5 in Toronto, at present represented by the hon. member for Davenport and part of which I represented when I first entered the house, part of it in the northwest, was almost an open field. The streets no-th of Queen and running west from Bathurst, Markham, Palmerston, Euclid, Manning, Shaw, from Queen to Bloor; all those streets for a mile and a half were built up by
Customs Tariff

houses erected in all these areas for the implement and other industries; also where the late Colonel Dennison, our magistrate, lived.
Under the protectionist policy that part of the city was built up. The workers bought their own homes and they did a great deal for Canada and for the British empire. I believe in protecting the farmer because he has had to suffer a lot in the past. Over ninety per cent of our industry owners were all right; but a small per cent of the manufacturers wanted to claim all the benefits of protection for themselves and give nothing in return to the consumer. After the war our own empire family should come first with Canada. The mother country wants to exchange goods and services along these lines.
Unless we and New Zealand and Australia help the mother country the British empire will go by default. I do hope that the Minister of Finance will declare before parliament closes what the policy of the government is going to be regarding preferences and empire trade all along the line when the war is over. If free trade has its way I believe that not tens of thousands but a million and a half of our population will have to go to the United States to look for work. You saw what happened at the Chicago convention last week, and there is another convention meeting there this week. A resolution was proposed that after the war they go for their own home market. I plead with the government to announce their policy regarding preferences and empire trade. Let the mother country know what you are going to do about them. These preferences should be brought up to date to meet modern conditions. Some of the duties are all right in some respects, but other duties undoubtedly should be protective. The United States and Russia are going to be the most highly protected countries in the world, war or no war. Britain has an agreement with Russia to-day, in which the dominions have no part, covering some of the matters to which I have referred to-night.

I had not intended to take part in this debate since I covered the ground pretty fully in speaking in the budget debate, but I could not let pass unchallenged the statement of the hon. member for Brantford City with respect to the cost of farm implements on the average farm. In twenty-five years of farming in western Canada it has cost me approximately $8,000 for farm machinery and repairs, or roughly $400 a year, which is considerably over the $1.65 suggested by the hon. member for Brantford City.

I said 3-3 per cent.
[Mr. Church. 1

That is 3-3 per cent of the average income. It certainly costs more than that in western Canada, and anyone who has farmed in Canada will bear me out in my figures as to the approximate cost of farm machinery on the average farm in the west.
This tariff item would be helpful in reducing farm machinery costs, provided always that the reduction in the tariff is carried through into the price of the machinery. But that has not happened in the west, and nobody knows it better than the present government. In 1935 they reduced the tariff from 25 per cent as it was under the Bennett government to 121 per cent, and promptly the price of farm machinery went up by 2-4 per cent. That certainly indicated to me, and I think to the people of Canada, that there was a combine in farm machinery as between the manufacturers in the United States and the manufacturers in Canada. Otherwise that reduction in the tariff should have been passed on to the user of farm machinery. I doubt whether this reduction in the tariff is going to mean very much unless the government are prepared to go farther than they have done in the past.
The hon. member for Brantford City said that he was alarmed about the position of labour. I have figures here as to what labour gets out of the total price paid by the farmer for farm machinery. These figures were produced before the committee which inquired into farm machinery prices in 1935 and 1936. On an 8-foot binder which cost the farmer $281 laid down in Regina, labour received $22.62, and that, I believe, included the full cost of factory labour and office staff also.
It did not take in any office staff. I was on that committee.

If it did not include the office staff I accept the hon. member's correction. The office staff may have been included in this other item of overhead, but it did include all the costs of factory labour. I would also point out that in the United States in 1939 farm implements were selling at approximately fifteen per cent below the Canadian price on an average, and yet United States factories were paying their labour from fifteen to twenty per cent more than was paid to labour in Canadian factories.
Mass production.

The Canadian factories should, have been working to their full capacity or perhaps they were overbuilt. Perhaps

Customs Tariff
their overhead was out of proportion to the trade which there was in Canada. So that I do not think the hon. member's arguments are very sound, and when he says that he is so much alarmed about labour I am inclined to believe that he is alarmed about other interests than labour.
I hope that the hon. member does not imply that about me too, because I certainly am concerned about labour.
If the cap does not fit, do not wear it.
He is pretty well alone on this side.
If I am right I do not mind if I am alone or not.

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to dumping duties. The tariff is being removed. Does that mean that any group of individuals or any individual in any part of Canada will be able to go to the United States and buy any type of farm implement or implement repairs and bring them into Canada absolutely free of duty of any kind? Suppose you are able to buy farm machinery or repair parts in the United States below the ordinary home consumption price in that country. Will the importer be compelled to pay a dumping duty on those goods when they enter Canada? Will they be valued for customs purposes at the ordinary price in the United States? Will dumping duties be applied?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been some years since I have given any consideration to the state of the law relating to dumping duties, but I think the dumping principle is still in our Customs Act. I think it is still a principle of our tariff laws that if goods are sold at less than the fair market value for home consumption in the country of origin, the dumping duty applies.

If that is the case, this tariff reduction may not be of much benefit to the Canadian farmer. I know we have cooperatives operating in western Canada today whose purpose it is to go to the United States and buy machines and repair parts on the cheapest market they can find.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
At a price less than the fair market value in the United States?
Mr. W'RIGHT: They may be able to make a bargain over there with certain firms to buy these repair parts at less than the fair market value as determined by the implement companies in the United States. They might be
able to make a bargain, for example, with Montgomery Ward or some other people who are not in the implement business to produce certain repair parts at considerably lower prices than are charged by the implement companies in the United States for those repairs; but if we have to pay the difference between the price which might be obtained by the cooperatives for these repairs and the price at which the implement companies consider a fair domestic price in the United States, this reduction in the tariff may not mean very much to the farmer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me say a word about that. The principle in the Customs Act is that if a foreign exporter quotes to a Canadian importer goods at a price less than the fair home market price of similar goods to a purchaser in that foreign country, the dumping duty applies. That is the principle of the dumping duty; it is to prevent dumping. The hon. gentleman apparently believes that the dumping of agricultural implements should be permitted. Does he believe that the dumping of butter from New Zealand should be permitted? I should like to find out about that.
That is a sixty-four dollar question.
Better think it over, anyway.

I am sure this does not present an appropriate opportunity to stage a first-class or full-dress debate on the question of the tariff structure. However, in view of what has been said here to-night, like the hon. member for Portage la Prairie I feel that I should put on record one or two comments.
I could have followed the hon. member for Brantford City, where farm implements are manufactured, had he stayed with his original argument, that it was a little unfair at this time, before the government had implemented its declared policy of exploring the world to improve the trade conditions of this country by entering into reciprocal trade agreements, to single out the farm implement industry in the matter of tariff reduction; that is, until the government in its general trade policy had dealt with a great many other items. But I noticed that to-night he went much farther; and as soon as the matter of cream separators was mentioned, I observed that the hon. member for Peterborough West, where cream separators are manufactured, rose in his place and protested against that particular tariff reduction. In addition, the hon. member for Broadview gave us to-night an argument, such as has been used ever since this question was first debated, against the step which the
Customs Tariff

government is taking. I hope the minister is not at all alarmed by the expressions of opinion on the part of these hon. members, all of whom have opposed this particular item in the budget changes. It was bound to come. As the Minister of Finance stated, as reported in Hansard, at page 4184:
However, the government desires to give concrete evidence of the direction which it is endeavouring to follow in the formulation of post-war commercial policy.
And on the same page, although not following immediately on that, he points out-
.	.	. the need for a bold initiative in the
orderly and agreed unshackling of world trade, if the ideals of economic expansion, higher incomes, full employment, adequate nutrition and the progressive abolition of poverty are to become realities.
I implore the minister never to hesitate or to weaken in the policy which he has declared to be the policy of the government in the post-war period, simply because one hon. member after another, when his particular baby is touched in this matter of unshackling trade-
Some day you will have a baby to be touched.

-thinks it is proper to rise in this chamber and protest against that particular item, which I hope is only one among a great many which will follow the same course, so that the objectives stated by the Minister of Finance may be reached, and the results of the Canada-First policy of 1930-35 will not only be undone, but the lessons we gathered as a result of that policy may be applied. In this way Canadian industry and Canadian agriculture will both prosper to a far greater degree than they can hope to do under any other policy which I have ever heard advocated in this house or outside it.

I should like to answer the question the minister asked me. It was a fairly direct question. I want to point out the difference between the conditions affecting farm machinery and those affecting butter. The price of farm machinery in the United States is set by a monopoly; it is fixed by people who control the price of farm machinery and are able to set it at any level they like. On the other hand butter is sold on the world market and must conform to the world price of butter, and it has always had to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would, I should think, be all the less reason for putting any duty against New Zealand butter. But there is always a great agitation when any butter

starts to come in. I have gone through this in previous years, and I know there is. Hon. members representing farming constituencies are always extremely vocal on that point. I just want to point out that I do not think we ought to get our legislation on an occupational or a class basis. We ought to realize that a principle should be applied all along the line, and I am afraid we do not. I know perfectly well what the attitude of hon. gentlemen would be if a large quantity of New Zealand butter were coming into this country: it would be to shut it out. I do not say we should, mind you. I think we should have a little consistency in our attitude toward these things; and the distinction the hon. member has drawn is a distinction without a difference. If there is a monopoly setting prices in the United States, how is your cooperative going to get a cut-rate price? You must bear in mind that we are talking about a condition which is perfectly non-existent at the present time and will be for a good long time to come. The difficulty is to get implements from the United States; the difficulty is not that of having implements dumped on us.

The cooperatives, by the way, are going into the United States and, along with the cooperatives in the United States, are buying a factory there and are going to manufacture their own implements for the cooperatives for distribution in both the United States and Canada; and if they are able to manufacture these implements at a considerably lower price than present manufacturing costs in the United States, then you propose to put on a dumping duty on them so as to bring prices up to United States prices, before they can be brought into Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think the dumping duty would apply in that case. I understand that if a manufacturer of these implements in the United States sells to a comparable purchaser in the United States at a price as low as the price he quotes to a purchaser in Canada, the article is not being dumped.
That puts a different complexion on the whole thing, if that is the case.

I think all of us are pleased at any benefit which may be derived from a change in the tariff on these items. If it results in a reduction of price to the farmer, hon. members, especially from the west, will gladly support it.
I dealt with this matter pretty carefully and, I think, clearly in speaking on the budget, and put on record figures which I obtained from the bureau of statistics and which the

Customs Tariff
hon. member for Brantford quoted this evening. As he stated in replying to a question I asked him, fifty per cent of the farmers' purchases of farm implements to-day consists of tractors, and they are on the free list. As the hon. member for Brantford City pointed out, when you take the average duty on the balance, it is so low that its effect will be very small indeed.
What I rose to say was that, while this may be a gesture to the farmer himself, I regret that the minister has not taken into consideration another individual who has much to do with the farms of western Canada, in fact, in the last three or four years, more than anyone else; I .mean the farmer's wife. I think the minister should have considered putting on the free list a great number of items which may be classified as household equipment on the farms, such as non-electrical refrigerators, vacuum cleaners and sweepers. Stoves might have been put on the list. The farmer's wife has been contending with the old stove. If things were made a little easier for her in that respect she would be tickled to death to get a new stove, an oil stove and so on. If you want to help the farmers, automobiles also might have been considered. Generally household equipment on the farm could have been considered and could have been put on the free list. In that way the one individual in the country who neeeds to be helped would have been helped.
You ought to join the Liberal party.
Those things are what I think could have been taken into consideration when the gesture was made by putting agricultural implements on the free list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid, if we had done that, my hon, friend would have said that we should have gone much farther, and many of his colleagues would have got up and said that we were turning men out of work. I think the safest policy is the policy I laid down in the budget, which is to look forward to arrangements which will have the effect of lowering world tariffs generally and promoting trade between nations. This is one step that we thought we should take for the reasons stated in the budget.

I find myself in a somewhat peculiar position to-night, because, after all, I represent an agricultural implement manufacturing riding. The Cockshutt Plow company happens to be in the constituency I have the honour to represent.
I may say that I cannot show the same concern as my colleague has in regard to what the future may have in store for the workingmen in the city of Brantford. I have been more or less following the stock markets, not that I have very great interest in them other than to see the trend of things, and I have discovered that there has been no reduction in the price of the stock of the agricultural implement companies. In fact in Tuesday's Globe and Mail I found that there has been a considerable increase in the stock of the Cockshutt Plow company on the stock exchange, which indicates that those who wish to put the product of their efforts in the form of money into that stock do not feel the same concern as do some hon. members of the committee. Furthermore, I wish to put myself on record as one of the hon. members supporting this government who believe that the policy of freer trade in all commodities of life is one of the solutions of our problems. We all boast about the things for which we are fighting. When the Atlantic charter was drafted by the great statesmen of the allied countries one of the clauses of that charter referred to the exchange of the natural resources and the goods of one nation with another.
I may say I am somewhat shocked at the attitude of the opposition. The hon. member for Broadview got up upon a high and lofty plane and tried to take under his wing the guidance and protection of the great British empire. I am not at all concerned about the British empire. The past record of the British empire shows that they have been well able to take care of themselves. There have been many people who prophesied the downfall of the British empire; but the fact of the matter is that that' empire has been always twenty years ahead of most of the other countries of the world. They have been well able to take care of themselves; and I still have confidence that it will not be necessary, particularly for Canada, to give any great preference to the products of Great Britain to enable it to maintain its existence. However, I feel that there are other things that should be considered. Personally I believe that the workingmen and the people that I have the honour to represent in the city of Brantford will be in a much better position under this particular policy than they will be under a restricted trade policy. We have had examples of high protection many a time. You have to look at the past and the path over which we have come to decide what the future may have in store for us if we follow certain policies.

What has been the result? I have before me the agricultural income of this country from 1926 to the present time. From 1926 to 1930 inclusive the average farm income in those five years was 8970,000.000. Then we had the blasting policy of our hon. friends across the way, who put on high tariffs and claimed that they were going to solve our problem. The result of that policy was that in the five years during which they had the privilege of administering the affairs of this country the average agricultural income dropped down to 8440,000,000, or less than one-half of what it was in the previous five years.

There was not a world
depression then.

The hon. member says that

Canada was still in this same old world as were the rest of the countries. In 1930 Canada stood in fifth place as a world trading nation. After five years of my hon. friend's policy we receded to seventh place as a trading nation in competition with all the rest of the world. There must have been something in that policy which made it impossible for the Canadian farmer to sell the product of his labours and relieve this market of goods. There must have been something in that policy which was responsible for depressing the prices in this country when the total agricultural income was less than one-half what it was in the previous five years. Now, then, to prove it to the hon. member-

There were high tariffs in
other countries which shut out our goods.

It cannot be mere coincidence that in 1935 the total agricultural income again was 1511,000,000 for that one particular year. However, I think it. is only fair to take the average. In the period from 1935 to 1940 we had two very bad years, 1937 and 1938. In those years we had practically a famine in the three prairie provinces so far as agricultural production was concerned. But let us include those years in the five-year period. In that five-year period we had a total agricultural production of 8675,000,000. In spite of the fact we had two of the worst years in the history of *his country so far as production is concerned; yet we had an increase of fifty per cent in returns to agriculture. Furthermore, for the benefit of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox, our trade in relation to other countries of the world had gone up until we were again the fifth trading nation of the

world at that particular time. At the present time we stand third Of course, part of that is due to the war, because some of the nations of the world are not in a position to compete with us. To-day Canada is filling that great place among the trading nations of the world. She is the greatest trading nation of the world for her population.
That brings me to this argument. Canada has proven in war time that her industry can compete with any other industry in any other country; and if it can be done in war time, why cannot it be done in peace time? Our productive possibilities have increased. We have three thousand more factories in Canada to-day than we had when the war broke out. Besides that, we have numerous other factories that have expanded their productive capacity. I do not see any reason why that productive capacity harnessed up cannot put Canada in a position to compete with the commerce of the world. I believe that it can be done, because if you remove those barriers- and many of those barriers militate against the manufacturer-the manufacturer will be able to participate in the benefits of a freer trade policy, and he will be able to produce cheaper.
I notice that under this particular item there are certain articles of iron and steel, rods and bars that are allowed to come in duty free. They go into the manufacture of agricultural implements. I might say that I do not take too seriously what the hon. member for Mel-fort said. He said, I think, that only 822 of labour entered into the manufacture of a binder.
Those figures were given to a committee of this house by the implement companies themselves.
I thought the hon. member said 822.
Yes, S22.62; that is the factory's labour cost.

But a great deal of the material going into a binder is already processed when it comes to the factory, and that labour must be taken into consideration. I do not think the figure mentioned by the hon. member for Melfort gives the proper relationship of the cost of labour to the price of the binder. I take the view that if Canada is to prosper in future, steps must be taken to keep the cost of production as low as possible. If there is one thing that will create

unemployment it is an increase in the cost of production, and that cost of production will be affected by the matter of wages. The best assurance labour can have as to its prosperity is a prosperous customer, and if the farmer is prosperous there is no doubt that the farm implement firms will be able to sell their products.
It has been argued that the benefit to the farmer as a result of the removal of this 7i per cent duty will be small. I have seen editorials in my local paper, as well as in the Globe and Mail, in which attempts were made to analyse the benefits that would go to the farmer, and I am shocked at their methods of arriving at a conclusion. As for my colleague the hon. member for Brantford City, while his legal ability may be great I am afraid his mathematics are bad. Let me tell the committee how I view this matter. Let us say that I purchase in the United States an agricultural implement costing $100. I have to pay $11 for United States currency, which brings the cost to $111. The duty on that implement is 7| per cent, which is figured not on $100 but on $111, which means an actual duty of $8.32. Up to the present there has been a war exchange tax of ten per cent, also assessed on the $111, which meant another $11.10. So that when you include the cost of exchange, the duty and the war exchange tax, that $100 implement will cost me $130.42, without any freight charges at all. It is true that we have no control over the $11 for exchange, but the removal of this duty will mean a benefit to the farmer of practically twenty per cent, consisting of $8.32 duty and $11.10 war exchange tax. I cannot see it in any other way. I obtained these figures from the department, and I believe this to be the correct picture. I am ready to admit that tractors have always come in free, and the only advantage we get there will be the removal of the ten per cent war exchange tax, which will be a considerable saving.
What was the amount stated by the hon. member for Melfort as the cost of labour in connection with a binder?
It was $22.62.

I suppose the average wage of a man working in a factory would not be less than $6 a day, which would mean that only three or four man-days would go into the manufacture of a binder. The idea is simply preposterous.
I only gave the figures of the companies, as they were presented to a select committee of this house in 1935.
If that represents your reasoning in all things, it is very inaccurate.

I thank the hon. member for Wellington South for drawing that point to the attention of the committee. Early in my remarks I endeavoured to direct attention to this rather ridiculous approach to this question.

The hon. member was in the house, I believe, at the time when the committee on the cost of agricultural implements was sitting. Did he question the figures of the companies at that time? I do not know whether the hon. member for Wellington South, who has just questioned my figures, was a member of the house at that time, but if he was he should have gone into those figures when they were placed on record by the implement companies themselves.
That is quite beside the point; I am not able to recall all the things I did ten years ago.
But at least you know a man could not make a binder in three or four days.

Yes, my common sense would tell me that. As I pointed out, that argument only gives part of the picture. That is characteristic of the group to which the hon. member for Melfort belongs. They generally say just enough to get people to believe what they want them to believe, without giving all the facts and facing realities. Of course they are just running true to form again. I will admit that it is good politics, because we cannot spend all our time in denying things. Most people know their arguments are ridiculous, but I have come to the conclusion that we have trusted the public too much and have allowed them to listen to the wild doctrines and statements of hon. members in the far comer for too long without giving the correct picture, because many people are coming to believe them. We thought most of our people were too intelligent to believe some of the ridiculous things hon. gentlemen in the far corner have been saying, but unfortunately, while engaged in the war effort, the people have not time to do their thinking properly, so that hon. gentlemen are having considerable success with their phoney arguments and policies.
I was going on to say that the discussion in regard to tractors has brought out the point that these machines are not manufactured in Canada, and I am sure the public will want to know why. At one time tractors were manufactured in the city of Brantford, but their design was rather cumbersome and did not meet with the approval of the buying public. As a result the company could not remain in business. To-day 'a tractor produces far more powder than it requires for its own
Customs Tariff

operation. The first tractors built in this country were so cumbersome that they required most of their power for their own operation, and had no reserve left. To-day tractors are so perfected that on level ground, by putting one's hand on a tractor one can push it along a level road. That is one type of progress that has been made.
I believe it was the hon. member for Broadview who drew attention to the fact that we would have to make our purchases from Great Britain and that to maintain herself she needed our business. Well, I have discovered that Great Britain drives a pretty hard bargain, when it comes to buying agricultural products. I am prepared to say that after this war is over we shall have to compete with Denmark in the British market, so far as our pork products and many other products are concerned. If we are going to compete satisfactorily, then the only answer the farmer has is that of reducing his costs of production. We cannot maintain high production costs, when those costs are far in excess of those in other countries, thereby placing the selling prices of our products beyond the reach of nations that are buying. This is all very well in war time, when there is very little competition, and when there is a ready market for everything. But some day we must face our Danish competitors on the bacon and cheese markets. The solution of our problem in Canada will be reached only by keeping down our production costs.
In the statement I made the other day in connection with sessional indemnities, I overlooked one point. May I say now that I take the view, and take it sincerely, that if Canada is to find a market for the products of her labour it will be necessary that we revise our thinking, and that we keep costs of production down so that those in other countries may be able to buy our produce.
The answer to higher wages and higher production costs will be met in unemployment; there can be no other answer. I say tliis because I feel it is important that the country should know where we stand, and where I stand particularly on this matter. The mere fact of lowering salaries or lowering wages does not necessarily mean that anyone is going to be deprived of what he needs. But if by lowering production costs we can increase the purchasing power of wages, wre at the same time are operating far more efficiently than if we have a continuous increase in prices, salaries and wages, and a resulting final increase in production costs.
To-day organized labour are demanding their rights. They have associated themselves, politically; and I warn labour definitely that 
if they continue this policy of accepting class legislation, they are heading for nothing short of disaster. Their experience will be paid for in unemployment.
There is only one way in which we can have prosperity, and that is by going abreast. If there is to be a national state, then the farmer has to have his place in the economic life of that state. He has carried the burden of other people too long, and he has now reached the point where he feels that he is entitled to some of those fine things, some of those good things in life. He feels that he has the same right to those things as the people who live in the more favoured industrial centres.
The great solution of our problems will be found in lowering production costs, so that when the farmer has to compete on the open markets of the world with the products of other countries he can compete and sell his surplus. In that way there will be a continuous market for his products. This is a long story, but I feel it my duty to state my position, and I want the people in my constituency to know where I stand on these matters.
The solution of our problems to-day rests in world trade. Canada to-day stands the greatest trading nation, according to her population of any country in the world. I believe that following a wise policy and with proper leadership along the road we have travelled in the last few years when Canada has become such a great nation, we shall maintain that position. By doing the wise thing I believe we can maintain the favourable position we enjoy to-day.

I came to this country thirty-six years ago, and I can well remember Sir Wilfrid Laurier sending his Minister of Finance, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, to the United States to negotiate a reciprocal agreement. I remember reading history to the effect that that was not the only budget of its kind Mr. Fielding had brought down. He had given Great Britain a preference before that time, a procedure which I approve. I remember that the agreement with the United States was put on the statute books of that country, and became an election issue in Canada, defeating the government. In my -opinion, as a man operating a farm in western Canada, that policy was fair not only for western Canada but for the whole of it.
As a result of a policy which was followed, lands and factories depreciated in value to a considerable extent. We have now reached the point where we are able to get back on our feet again, and to enjoy some real Liberalism. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) asked a question yesterday which I promised to answer to-morrow. I have the information and I will answer the question now. In regard to complete equipment imported after June 26 of this year the lawful price must be reduced to the full extent of the exchange tax and/or duties removed by the budget. This means that prices of floor stocks of complete equipment are not reduced by law, although undoubtedly the ordinary process of competition will have an influence. Arrangements have been made to tag specially every piece of complete equipment imported prior to June 26. Inventory of complete equipment is not in any event very large since these machines have been on a hand-to-mouth basis for some considerable time after the wartime prices and trade board's rationing procedure.
That is the situation with regard to complete equipment imported after June 26. To summarize, it wTould appear to me that the situation is that on what they had already imported before June 26 they may include the war exchange tax and duty and charge that in their price, but on what they import after June 26 they cannot. There is to be a separation of the goods.
The hon. gentleman said that at the time the war exchange tax went on, the amount was added to the price of the goods that had already been imported. Is that correct?

Yes. I know of a case
where the article, a tractor, was imported before the war exchange tax went on, and when they sold the tractor they added the war exchange tax to the selling price. Complaint was made about it, and they showed 
it exactly as the war exchange tax, although they had never paid the tax to the government. The officials of the national revenue department said that they could sell the tractor at any price they wanted at that time. Therefore it would appear that at that time they were able to add the tax to the price of the article. Now, when their inventories are even lower, they are protected against the tax being taken off the price. I suggest that the rule be made to apply both ways, and that where it can be shown that any company charged the tax when it did not actually pay it, the revenue officials of the government should see to it that the tax is refunded to the people who actually paid it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That sounds very fair to
me and I made inquiries 'to-day to find out if that had been the case. Apparently it was not generally the case when the war exchange tax was imposed in 1940. It may have been done in some individual instances. I do not know whether it would be possible to isolate those instances. It was forbidden by the law. If the hon. gentleman will look at the Special War Revenue Act, chapter 41 of the statutes of 1939, which became the law on August 7, 1940, he will find this provision:
No person shall take advantage of the tax imposed by this section to increase the price of goods by an amount greater than is justified by any increase in cost properly arising from such tax or to maintain prices at levels higher than are so justified and, where the wartime prices and trade board reports to the governor in council that, in its opinion, any person has so taken advantage, the governor in council may, upon the recommendation of the said board, for such period of time as he may determine, impose upon all or any of the goods produced, sold or dealt in by such person an excise tax at a rate not to exceed ten per cent of the selling price of such goods, remove or reduce customs duties applicable thereto, fix the prices thereof and take or authorize the said board to take such other measures under the wartime prices and trade board regulations as the said board may recommend.
As I read that, there may be two inter-[DOT]pretations. I have not given much thought to the interpretation, but as I read it an importer who had on hand goods on August 7, 1940, and who added to the prices of the stock that he had on hand the amount of the war exchange tax as a part of the price which he had not paid, would be taking advantage of the tax to increase the price of the goods by an amount greater than justified by any increase in price properly arising from such tax. But it is susceptible of another interpretation. It might apply to persons who paid only ten per cent duty and tried to raise the price by fifteen per cent. That may be the meaning, but whatever its meaning

I am informed by the former chairman of the wartime prices and trade board that he can remember no complaints to him about it, and certainly there was no recommendation by the prices board to the governor in council to exercise the punitive powers authorized by the section. I am still talking about complete equipment, complete tractors, for example.
Here is a memorandum I have from the wartime prices and trade board:
We are informed that there was a wide variation in what was done by the industry. Furthermore, the percentage added varied as between individual parts, with the result that the additions made were larger in some eases than in others, but on the whole the overall addition was somewhat lower than was justified. It should be particularly noted that there was a time lag of about two months before the industry adjusted any prices.
I gather that that refers to goods imported on which the war exchange tax was paid. I now come to the treatment of parts. The memorandum says:
That in regard to "parts" brought in either before or after June 26-the lawful price must be reduced after September 30. It will be noted that this provision includes floor stocks so that on October 1 the lawful maximum price of all parts must be reduced.
The reasons for this procedure are as follows:
This is the first time that following a removal of taxes or duties the government has required a reduction in established prices. Heretofore the reduction took place under force of competition. Under the board order it should be noted that we are dealing with legal maximum prices. There is nothing to prevent the operation of the ordinary forces of competition.
I should say at this stage that perhaps the ordinary forces of competition are not working now. If we rely on government action only, we must take action that is practicable.
The next reason is as follows:
It seemed manifestly unfair to force importers and dealers to take a loss on taxes and duties already paid. True, in pre-price ceiling days they might have had the risk of loss, but that is quite different to compelling the loss. When war exchange tax went on in 1940, importers and dealers were not prevented from increasing prices, but section 6 of the War Exchange Conservation Act provided for a penalty tax if undue advantage were taken.
I might interject that I think they were prevented from increasing prices on what they had already imported. The memorandum goes on:
So far as we know, this tax was never imposed so that we must assume that no undue advantage was taken.
The hon. gentleman says that in individual cases undue advantage was taken. It goes on:
In fact, we are informed that there was a wide variation in what was done by the industry. Furthermore, the percentage added varied as between individual parts, with the result
that the additions made were larger in some cases than in others, but on the whole the overall addition was somewhat lower than was justified. It should be particularly noted that there was a time lag of 'about two months before the industry adjusted any prices.
I read that passage before. The memorandum goes on:
There are at least 75,000 to 80,000 parts involved on which new prices have to be worked out. It is a physical impossibility to revise the various price lists in less than the time allowed. It would have been impossible to segregate the parts received after June 26 or to tag all the items so that a two-price system could be established to differentiate those in inventory before and after that date. Moreover, such a two-price system was considered highly inadequate in any event and the decision to reduce the price of all parts on a specific date not only gives the hoard some chance to police its regulations hut also eliminates confusion for the consumer. Under any two-price system enforcement seemed impossible and unscrupulous dealers would take advantage of the situation. As part of the arrangement the industry agrees to absorb any loss on all floor stocks after the specific date.
If in fact we had attempted to compel the industry to reduce prices they could quite properly have asked us to name the specific reduction on each item which would have required an examination of each of the 80,000 items for each company to establish what actual additions took place for the exchange tax in 1940 and duties in earlier years. Any effort to meet the situation by a general order as we attempted to in order No. 419, later cancelled, left us with such a lack of definiteness that enforcement seemed impossible. Moreover, we could scarcely have refused to entertain requests for the payment of subsidies in accordance with general policy.
The stock of parts on hand at June 26 was considered to be much heavier than the quantities which can be imported before September 30 in view of quota allocations. Therefore, it seemed to the benefit of the farmers to get all stocks of parts reduced by September 30 than to continue with the higher price during the entire liquidation period-perhaps years-of the pre-June 26 inventory.
The September 30 date should give small dealers a reasonable opportunity to dispose of inventory. There are over ten thousand of such dealers most of whom simply could not absorb 'the reduction and subsidies would have had to be paid.
Obviously any farmer is put in the position by our order that by simply withholding his purchases of parts until October 1, he can ensure lower prices.
That is, if he can do so. And the information I have is that most repair work takes place after harvest.
Those are the reasons given for the action taken. The board was confronted with quite a problem with regard to these parts. The old rule about putting on duties and taking off duties was that when you put on duties the person in this country who was stocked up with the article on which the duties were

increased got the benefit, and when the duties were taken off the person who was stocked up suffered a loss. Competition made him suffer a loss. Well now, the forces of competition are free to work here, if they will work, and if they have to be supplemented by government order, which we are doing, the government order apparently cannot take effect at once because there is this huge number of items, 80,000 items, the price of every one of which has to be examined and an order made in respect of it. I do not know whether the situation is very satisfactory; it seems to have been the best the board could do with it.

I wish to say in that regard that I have received a very bitter complaint about the wartime prices and trade board putting out order No. 419, which some implement agencies communicated to their customers and then heard over the radio of its cancellation, leaving them so that they do not know where they are at. In order that we may soften the fears of the hon. member for Brantford City that the implement manufacturers in his constituency may be put out of business, I should like to tell a story. This is a true story, one which happened in Toronto within the last six months. A manufacturer in that city who along with his regular business has a contract with the wartime prices and trade board was visited by one of the engineers. Apparently this manufacturer sold his goods within a certain freight zone, one which extended, I be^ lieve, about 350 or 400 miles. He said to the engineer, "Do you think I can sell my goods in the city of Quebec?" The engineer said, "Why do you wish to go as far as Quebec?" The engineer had1 in his pocket a set of callipers, placing one point on Toronto, where it appeared on the map, and drew a circle with a radius of 350 miles around that city. That circle took in about 35,000,000 people in the United States. The engineer said, "Did it ever occur to you that you might explore the possibilities of that market over there?" The manufacturer replied with the question, "Do you think I could sell my goods in the United States.?" "Well," said the engineer, "I would try." "What would you advise me to do," said the manufacturer. "I would advise you to get your No. 1 salesman to go along with you, and go prepared to stay for two or three months and see what happens." That engineer was back in Toronto three months later, when the manufacturer, upon meeting him, said, "Well, I did what you told me. I made my trip to the United States, and I have returned. I could have sold more goods in six weeks over there than I sold in Canada in the past three years."
Does that sound much like the suggestion that Canadian manufacturers would be put out of business by tariff reductions? I do not think so. I do not think the hon. member for Brantford City is fair with his manufacturing friends in Brantford. There never was one vestige of evidence given in this house, during the twenty years I have been here, to prove that Canadian manufacturers could not always and at all times and in every respect compete with the United States. I think we can do a better job, because I think our Canadian people are more ingenious and

we have better and cheaper power in Canada and a greater store of natural resources, and of those things required to produce manufactured goods.
My suggestion to the government would be that in the very near future it should move to destroy all trade restrictions between this country and the United States, or any other part of the world. If we hope to give full employment after the war, the only basis upon which we can proceed is that of complete free trade throughout the world. As there has been in connection with the distribution of munitions of war, there must continue to be an exchange between one country and another, without tariff restriction. That is the thing that will put our people to work. I hope the time is not far distant when we may see that happy day in Canada.
I have only one more word, and that is in reference to the effect this tariff reduction will have upon the Canadian agricultural economy. In 1937 I made an extensive trip into the United States, covering many thousands of miles, and I did so for the purpose of drawing a comparison between costs in the United States and Canada of machinery used by farmers. What did I find? I travelled as far as Missouri, passing through seven or eight states, and talking with farmers all along the way. I discussed implement prices not only with farmers but with small dealers in the villages and towns, as I drove along. At that time I found that there was an average difference of about eighteen per cent between the cost of machines in Canada and in the United States. It will be recalled that at that time there was a fifteen per cent duty on farm machinery. There was almost an exact parallel in price levels between Canada and the United States when the 15 per cent duty andi excise was added.
What does this mean? It proves beyond doubt that there is an international combine; there can be no doubt about that. I do not think anybody would argue that there is not to-day a water-tight international eom-bine in respect of implement manufacturing. It is all-embracing. It embraces the whole continent, and we must get that point clear. I believe, however, that with this tariff reduction we now have we dhall enjoy the whole benefit of the reduction, because I found in the United States that the price of farm machinery there, was, as I say, eighteen per cent below

I think it holds great possibilities for us, even though there is an international combine. It may materially affect the growth of our cooperatives because I believe this reduction will prove of great value to them. A factory has recently been purchased by the cooperative societies of the United States in which the Canadian wholesale implement cooperative people are interested. If we as farmers can show that we know how to help ourselves we shall be able to prove to what extent this international combine is bleeding the farmers on the north American continent. The United States farmer is being bled along with the Canadian farmer. The United States farmer is suffering with us, in fact I am not so sure that he is not suffering more because his wage costs are higher, his taxes are higher, and many of the things he has to buy are higher. I feel that our Canadian manufacturers will still be able to manufacture in free competition with the United States.

If the members of the official nnposition who have spoken on this item tonight are representing their leader, we must take it that Mr. Bracken is not a free trader but a high protectionist.

Item agreed to.
Items 409. 409a, 409b, 409c, 409d, 409e, 409f, 409g, 409h, 409i, 409j and 409k agreed to.
Customs tariff-J09n. Portable engines with boilers, in combination, for farm purposes: horse powers; complete parts of all the foregoing: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, free; general tariff, free.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: I do not see small stationary gasoline engines in this list. Are they to come in duty free for farm purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
They ought to be included
in the free list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: They are not agricultural implements.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: They are certainly used a* much as any agricultural implement. They are used for running the fanning mill, for pumping water, for pressure tanks, for milking machines and for many other purposes on the farm. I see that small gasoline engines to be attached to electric lighting equipment are allowed to come in free, but apparently the small stationary gasoline engine which is so commonly used on the farm is not on the free list. It is a very important agricultural implement. It is used extensively on the farm, and certainly it should be on the free list for agricultural purposes. I am not arguing for its free entry for other purposes, but it certainly' should enter free when used for agricultural purposes because it is an important implement of production.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: It is one of the greatest labour savers on the farm, saving the labour of men and of women too. It is hooked up to several implements on the farm, and I should like to see it included in the free list.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
They have never been included in the schedules of agricultural implements. The rate of 7i per cent applied to practically all agricultural implements. The tariffs on engines is an entirely different matter. I would not want to touch this tariff on engines without an exhaustive investigation. You cannot make changes just as simply as that. That is somewhat like the suggestion of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who wanted us to put on the free list a great range of household machinery. I made it clear in my budget speech that this is not a far-reaching tariff revision at all. I made it clear that we were taking one class of items, the kind of things always regarded as agricultural
Customs Tariff

implements and machinery, which have always included cream separators, but have never included gasoline engines. It would be out of the question to put them on the free list for farmers alone, because there are so many other people who would be entitled to similar treatment.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: I object to the sarcastic way in which the minister has referred to me two or three times to-night and on other occasions. I have been sincere in every suggestion I have made. On this point I wish to say that this stationary gas engine has been handled by all implement dealers in western Canada for a great number of years. I myself was connected with an implement firm twenty years ago; we handled these engines and sold several of them. They were part of our agricultural implement trade. While I was home at Easter I tried to buy one of these engines to put over a well to pump water. The windmill had blown down, and instead of building a new windmill, which we could not get free of duty and could1 not obtain material for, I bought a new engine and had to pay a very high duty on it. So that I think this is a very important matter. I agree with hon. members to the left that the minister should consider putting this on the free list, because it certainly will help the farmers more than almost anything else one can think of.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: If the minister after a thorough investigation objects to putting all stationary engines on the free list, I suggest that he make this concession in respect of engines up to three horsepower, because it is the one to three horse-power type of engine which is generally in use on small farms.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: The minister does bring in gasoline engines for agricultural tractors. He makes a distinction there. I cannot just follow his reasoning in refusing to allow us to bring in small stationary engines used for agricultural purposes, while one can bring in tractors used for agricultural purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
Tractors have always been on the free list; these other engines have never been. There are quite a number of small, competent, efficient industries in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific manufacturing gasoline engines; and it would be, as I say, entirely unjust to pick out a class used by farmers alone and make those free, because there are other importers who would be equally entitled to consideration, and I should not like to do a piece of tariff-tinkering like that at this time, without much further investigation than it has been possible to give. That comes within the general range of our tariff policy, which is to try to arrange a 
reciprocal basis and get world tariffs down. These engines have never been included with agricultural implements. They bear a different rate from that on agricultural implements. It would be impossible in justice to segregate one class of these engines in that way, and I cannot entertain the suggestion.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: Just before the item carries, in the very next item, 409o, "Equipment for generating electric power for farm purposes only, viz.: engine", is the first item that is mentioned; and that would be practically the same thing that these hon. members are talking about, would it not?

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: The fact that this has never been included in the free list before is no excuse for not including it, because to-day we have people dying who never died before. I think the minister might change his mind with regard to these small gas engines, because certainly they are one of the most necessary farm implements we have at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: This item 409o has always been included in the group known as agricultural machinery and implements. It is true that the rate from the United States has been ten per cent instead of 7J per cent, but it has always been included in that group and it is limited to farms. It is equipment for generating electric power for farm purposes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: What kind of engines are referred to in 409n? Steam engines?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: They would be steam engines, yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: But there too, they are segregated: "for farm purposes."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: I might point out with reference to 409d, these semi-stationary engines, if they are attached to a combine, are allowed in free.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: They are part of the combine then, are they not?

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: They are a separate engine which sits on the frame of the combine and drives the combine. They are a stationary gasoline engine; they can take them off and use them for other purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: But they are part of the combine.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
I think the difficulty we over here are experiencing is to understand the minister's objecting to segregate gasoline engines for farm purposes when there is this segregation for farm purposes with respect to two or three other items.

Privilege-M r. Gray don

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: It has been done for a long time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext:
People are doing things now which they have not done for a long time.
Mr. LaFLECHE: I think the C.C.F. are never done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: I cannot open up that gasoline engine item without much more investigation than has been possible so far.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: I suggest that the minister sleep on it and give us a little better encouragement to-morrow-give us free gasoline engines.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: It will not be to-morrow, I can assure my hon. friend.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: There are many of these gasoline engines used in connection with dairying in western Canada. Every dairy farm has one of these gasoline engines, and they will wear them out quicker than any other piece of equipment. Every farmer needs them to-day for cooling milk, for putting water through the cooler. If you want to benefit the farmer by reducing tariffs, bear in mind that this is one article which we have to replace oftener than anything else which we must have.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: I respectfully suggest that the minister let this item stand until he has given the matter a little more consideration, and he will perhaps change his mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: I cannot change my mind on this item of gasoline engines. I have given it much consideration; and the situation is such that I will not, I must say firmly, carve out an additional item on gasoline engines for farm use or for any particular use. Hon. gentlemen are trying to drive me a little too far on this. We have taken the usual list of agricultural implements and have put them on the free list, and I have given the reasons for doing that. Naturally we could spend a long time here in saying that it would be nice to have this free and nice to have that free, and do it here in the house, without reference to the many ramifications which such an action would have. But I certainly cannot take the responsibility of doing so.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: What is the reason for not putting gasoline engines on the free list?

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: Half the farmers in western Canada have one.

subtopic: SCHEDULE OF MANUFACTURING COSTS OF AN 8-FT. BINDER AS COMPARED WITH GRAIN PRICES
speechtext: Do not wait another twenty-five years.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
